add: Add the main reproductive organs and body-safety rules.
point: Names the main reproductive organs and body-safety rules.

evidence: infectious vs non-infectious diseases, sorted
point: Explains infectious and non-infectious diseases and sorts common diseases into them.

evidence: the road each common germ travels; mosquito spread
point: Explains how diseases spread through water, food, mosquitoes, air and blood.

evidence: rehydration drink needs salt and sugar
add: Name signs of dehydration and give the ORS recipe.
point: Names signs of dehydration and how to make oral rehydration solution.

evidence: how HIV attacks the immune system
add: Explain HIV does not spread by touch, hugging, shared food or mosquitoes.
point: Explains that HIV does not spread by touch, hugging, shared food or mosquitoes.

evidence: causes of diabetes; common diseases
add: Explain how lifestyle links to heart disease, stroke, diabetes and cancer.
point: Explains how lifestyle affects heart disease, stroke, diabetes and cancer.

evidence: vaccines, mosquito nets, washing wounds
point: Lists the main ways to protect against disease.

evidence: wet and dry waste; segregation; sort degradable
point: Sorts household waste into degradable and non-degradable, with reasons.

evidence: burnt waste goes into the air; dumping harms soil and water
point: Explains why dumping or burning waste harms soil, water, air and health.

evidence: segregation, composting and disposal
point: Describes proper disposal: segregation, composting and recycling.

evidence: disposal and reuse; hard-to-recycle materials
point: Explains recycling and reuse with examples.

evidence: name hazardous waste and e-waste; where each goes
point: Explains that some waste, such as batteries and medicines, is hazardous.

evidence: caring for each other and for places
add: Explain how to help keep a public place clean.
point: Takes part in keeping public places clean.

evidence: xylem carries water up, phloem carries food
point: Plants move water from the roots and food from the leaves to other parts through tubes.

evidence: fish gills and human lungs
add: Add plants taking in oxygen and giving out carbon dioxide.
point: Air is a mix of gases, and plants, fish and humans all take in oxygen and give out carbon dioxide.

evidence: lungs, gills, heart and blood vessels work together
point: The breathing system (nose, windpipe, lungs) and circulatory system (heart, blood, blood vessels) each have parts that work together to carry out life processes.

evidence: pollination, fertilisation, seed dispersal, germination; spores
point: Flowering plants make seeds through pollination, fertilisation, seed dispersal and germination, and some plants reproduce with spores.

evidence: fertilisation: egg and sperm
add: Compare with plant fertilisation after pollination.
point: In humans, a sperm fuses with an egg, and the fertilised egg develops in the womb, a process similar to fertilisation in flowering plants.

evidence: melting points; reversible changes
add: Give water's 0 and 100 C points and the heat that changes its state.
point: Water exists as ice, liquid and steam, and it changes state at 0 C and 100 C as heat is gained or lost.

evidence: wider surface loses more water; what speeds drying
point: Evaporation is faster with more wind, higher temperature and a larger exposed surface area, which children can investigate.

evidence: evaporation and condensation in the water cycle
point: Evaporation and condensation drive the water cycle, which matters for all life on Earth.

evidence: kinds of water pollution; pollutants build up in food chains
point: Water is essential to life processes, and water pollution reduces the quality of Earth's water resources.

evidence: bulbs and cells in a loop
add: Teach a closed circuit with a switch and sort conductors from insulators at Class 5 depth.
point: A battery, wires, bulb and switch form an electrical system, and current flows only when the circuit is closed.

evidence: series and parallel bulbs; cells in a circuit
point: The current in a circuit changes with the number of batteries and bulbs, and with whether they are arranged in series or parallel.

evidence: repeat and average; conclusion says no more than numbers
add: Add changing one variable and testing explanations against evidence.
point: Children investigate one variable at a time, use data to test ideas, and check explanations against evidence.

add: Explain how conditions differ between habitats and microhabitats.
point: Habitats and microhabitats differ in temperature, light and water, and these conditions shape which living things can live there.

evidence: cactus spines and waxy skin fit the desert; adaptations
point: Plants are suited to their environment, so their adaptations let us predict the habitat where a plant is likely to grow.

evidence: plants of the Thar desert vs the wet forest
point: Children compare the features of plant adaptations in two contrasting habitats.

evidence: sort soluble and insoluble
add: Add sieving to separate solids in a mixture.
point: Some solids can be mixed, and sieving separates some mixtures.

evidence: salt disappears into water; flour does not
add: Explain filtration of insoluble solids with filter paper.
point: Filtration separates insoluble solids such as sand from a liquid, because liquids pass through filter paper and solids do not.

evidence: salt disappears into water
add: Explain why filtration cannot separate salt from water.
point: Soluble solids such as sugar and salt form a solution that filtration cannot separate.

evidence: stir both glasses; one clears
add: Test how crushing, heating and stirring speed up dissolving.
point: Crushing, heating or stirring makes simple substances such as sugar and salt dissolve faster, and children compare amounts that dissolve.

evidence: evaporation with particles
add: Explain recovering a dissolved solid by evaporating the liquid.
point: When a solution is left in the air, the liquid evaporates and the dissolved solid is left behind.

evidence: sort soluble and insoluble
add: Choose a separation method (sieve, magnet, filter, evaporate) for each mixture.
point: Knowing how solids, liquids and gases behave helps decide how to separate mixtures by sieving, magnets, filtering or evaporating.

evidence: light travels in straight lines; ray diagram
point: Light comes from a source and travels in straight lines, and we see objects that give out or reflect light into our eyes.

evidence: shiny and dull surfaces; light from surfaces tracked
add: Explain why smooth shiny surfaces reflect light better than dull ones.
point: Light reflects from shiny surfaces and changes direction, and smooth shiny surfaces reflect light better than dull ones.

evidence: see-through and opaque materials
point: Transparent materials let light pass through, and opaque materials do not.

evidence: planets of the solar system and Earth
add: Say the Sun is a star at the centre of the Solar System.
point: The Sun is a star at the centre of the Solar System, and Earth is a planet with one moon.

evidence: Earth spins once in 24 hours
add: Add the Moon orbiting Earth and planets orbiting the Sun (link sci.gravity.orbits.L5).
point: Earth spins on its axis, which causes day and night, while the Moon orbits Earth and the planets orbit the Sun.

evidence: shadows (L2 level)
add: Explain why shadow length changes and the Sun's apparent movement.
point: Shadow length changes during the day, and the Sun's apparent movement across the sky is caused by Earth's rotation.

evidence: Ptolemy's epicycles; Earth-centred and Sun-centred models
point: Ideas about the Solar System changed over time, from Ptolemy's Earth-centred model to Copernicus's Sun-centred model.

evidence: odd result spotted, checked and not hidden
add: Add naming a test's limits and suggesting a better method.
point: Children name the limits of an investigation, suggest improvements, and spot results that look odd or do not fit the pattern.

evidence: conclusion with claim, evidence and reasoning
add: Add predicting a new value from results.
point: Children draw simple conclusions from results, predict new values, and identify evidence that supports or refutes a conclusion.

evidence: stored energy in cells and springs changes form
add: Add renewable sources that are renewed by Sun, wind and water.
point: Energy can be stored and changed from one form to another, and some energy sources can be renewed.

evidence: pulleys and gears trade a smaller pull for a longer distance
point: Simple machines such as gears let people move things with less force, and people still use simple machines today.

evidence: fertilisers, medicines, fuels and paints come from chemistry
add: Weigh a benefit and an environmental cost of changing a material.
point: People change materials to suit their needs, and manufacturing has benefits, challenges and environmental effects.

evidence: producers use sunlight; removing one link affects others
point: Solar energy sustains ecosystems by passing along food webs, so changing one link affects the others.

evidence: DNA; why siblings differ; inheritance
add: Compare how different living things reproduce, in a life-cycle unit.
point: Living things reproduce in different ways as part of a life cycle, and genetics affects which features are inherited.

evidence: planets and the solar system scale
add: Explain stars as navigation guides and how solar-system events affect Earth.
point: Regular events in the solar system, such as day, night and seasons, affect Earth, and stars help with navigation.

evidence: vaccines prepare the body
add: Explain how vaccines and healthy choices protect others, not only ourselves.
point: Vaccinations and responsible choices protect our own health and the health of others.

evidence: repeat, average and conclusion from results
add: Plan a systematic investigation and test a prediction.
point: Children plan systematic investigations, change one variable, and make and test predictions to draw conclusions.

evidence: Some families are big, with grandparents, aunts and cousins under one roof.
point: Families come in many sizes and forms, and a family can have few or many members.
ref: Unit 1, Chapter 1: Family and Friends

evidence: A family is a group of people who look after each other.
point: Family, friends and neighbours love, care for and support one another.
ref: Unit 1, Chapter 1: Family and Friends

evidence: Work that nobody pays money for, such as cooking for your own family
point: Families share the daily housework, and children help with tasks such as cooking, cleaning, shopping and gardening.
ref: Unit 1, Chapter 1: Family and Friends

evidence: English has one word, uncle, for four different relations.
point: Relatives are linked to us through our parents, and families use different names for the same relative.
ref: Unit 1, Chapter 1: Family and Friends

evidence: I can treat animals kindly while I watch them, and explain why we should not disturb a nest.
point: Families love and care for animals, plants and trees, and pets can be family members.
ref: Unit 1, Chapter 1: Family and Friends

add: NOT SCIENCE: games children play with elders (antakshari, pitthoo) belong in a family or social unit.
point: Families play games together indoors and outdoors, and older people pass on the games they played as children.
ref: Unit 1, Chapter 1: Family and Friends

add: NOT SCIENCE: rainy-day family customs, pakodas and songs are social, not science; drop from the science map.
point: On rainy days families sit together under a shelter, eat pakodas and sing songs learned from elders.
ref: Unit 1, Chapter 1: Family and Friends

evidence: In the North and West a similar pattern, often coloured, is called a rangoli.
point: Families and friends celebrate festivals and share food, and friends help one another with crafts.
ref: Unit 1, Chapter 1: Family and Friends

add: NOT SCIENCE: children learning from elders and teaching others is social; belongs in family or language unit.
point: Children learn many things from family members and neighbours, and can also teach others.
ref: Unit 1, Chapter 1: Family and Friends

add: NOT SCIENCE: a shared park outing is social; rest and ball physics are science but already covered elsewhere.
point: A day out to the park with friends and an elder is a joyful shared activity that includes rest and treats.
ref: Unit 1, Chapter 1: Family and Friends

add: NOT SCIENCE: packing and planning a trip is social; drop from the science map.
point: Families prepare for a trip by packing essentials such as water bottles and a special bag, and they plan the route.
ref: Unit 1, Chapter 2: Going to the Mela

add: NOT SCIENCE: neighbours helping elders travel is social; not a science point.
point: Families and neighbours travel together and look out for one another, especially older members.
ref: Unit 1, Chapter 2: Going to the Mela

evidence: such as a bus, a cycle, an auto, a boat or an aeroplane.
point: Different vehicles, such as trains, city buses and autorickshaws, carry people in towns and cities.
ref: Unit 1, Chapter 2: Going to the Mela

evidence: A red circle with a crossed-out horn means 'Do not sound your horn here'.
add: Add how to cross a road safely (look both ways) and why to keep hands and head inside a bus.
point: Road and bus safety: cross carefully, watch vehicles from both sides, sit down and keep hands and heads inside.
ref: Unit 1, Chapter 2: Going to the Mela

evidence: I can describe a mela: what the stalls and toys are made of, who works there
point: A mela has many stalls and activities, such as toys, games, sweets, rides and a magic show.
ref: Unit 1, Chapter 2: Going to the Mela

evidence: Washing your hands with soap before you eat is hygiene.
point: Food and hygiene at a mela: wash hands at the water point before eating, and put waste in the dustbin.
ref: Unit 1, Chapter 2: Going to the Mela

evidence: I can say what public services such as a government school, a health centre
add: Add the mela's ambulance, police jeep, fire engine and lost-and-found booth, and what each does.
point: A mela has services such as an ambulance, a police jeep, a fire engine and a lost and found booth.
ref: Unit 1, Chapter 2: Going to the Mela

evidence: why a neighbourhood needs so many different jobs
point: A police dog helps the police officer, and the people at a mela have many jobs such as a halwai, toy seller or firefighter.
ref: Unit 1, Chapter 2: Going to the Mela

add: NOT SCIENCE: add Kumbh Mela to the festivals unit: held every 12 years on river banks at four places.
point: Kumbh Mela is the world's biggest gathering, held on the banks of rivers every 12 years at four places.
ref: Unit 1, Chapter 2: Going to the Mela

evidence: draw maps of your room, your home and your street.
point: Maps show where places are, and a sketch can show the route from home to school.
ref: Unit 1, Chapter 2: Going to the Mela

evidence: I can describe a mela: what the stalls and toys are made of, who works there
add: Add a class mock mela: planned stalls, roles and play money using local materials.
point: Children can organise a mock mela in class with stalls, roles and play money using local materials.
ref: Unit 1, Chapter 2: Going to the Mela

evidence: A vehicle is a machine that carries people or goods, such as a bus
add: Add a hill bus trip: hairpin bends, mountains and tall trees, and the safety rules on the bus.
point: Travel by bus shows safety rules and features of the road, such as hairpin turns, mountains and tall trees.
ref: Unit 1, Chapter 3: Celebrating Festivals

evidence: A road sign is a board by the road that gives a message with
add: Add No Parking, Speed Breaker and Men at Work signs; children match them to meanings and draw new ones.
point: Road safety: signboards tell us rules and warnings, such as No Parking, Speed Breaker and Men at Work.
ref: Unit 1, Chapter 3: Celebrating Festivals

evidence: Why do white clothes and reflective strips keep a walker safe at night?
point: Walking and cycling safety: know the rules for the road and be careful while riding or walking.
ref: Unit 1, Chapter 3: Celebrating Festivals

evidence: Some flowers, such as tulips and crocuses, open when they get warm
add: Add which flowers bloom in which season and place: rose, marigold, hibiscus, tulip, buransh.
point: Flowers of different places: rose, marigold, hibiscus, tulip and rhododendron (buransh) bloom in different seasons.
ref: Unit 1, Chapter 3: Celebrating Festivals

evidence: A woman drawing a white dotted kolam on the floor at a doorstep in the early morning.
add: Add spring festivals with doorstep flowers, rituals and sweets; compare customs across regions.
point: Spring festivals across India: people put flowers on doorsteps, make rituals and share food and sweets.
ref: Unit 1, Chapter 3: Celebrating Festivals

evidence: You learn the foods, clothes and customs of festivals from Kerala to Assam.
add: Add Vishu in Kerala and Sarhul in Jharkhand, with their foods and offerings to Earth and Sun.
point: Festivals in different states have their own names, food and rituals, such as Vishu in Kerala and Sarhul in Jharkhand.
ref: Unit 1, Chapter 3: Celebrating Festivals

evidence: Vasanta ritu is spring, and Varsha ritu is the rainy season.
add: Add spring after winter: flowers, new leaves and sunshine, and why people celebrate it.
point: Seasons shape the way people celebrate: after winter, spring brings flowers, new leaves and sunshine.
ref: Unit 1, Chapter 3: Celebrating Festivals

evidence: You learn the foods, clothes and customs of festivals from Kerala to Assam.
point: Festival food and dress differ from place to place, and each festival has special food and clothes.
ref: Unit 1, Chapter 3: Celebrating Festivals

evidence: often with special food, clothes, prayers, music and decoration
point: Festivals bring people together through food, music, dance, dress and shared joy.
ref: Unit 1, Chapter 3: Celebrating Festivals

evidence: It was later named Everest.
add: Add Himalayas in northern India, Everest in Nepal, about 8,848 metres high.
point: Mountains and peaks: the Himalayas are in northern India and Mount Everest lies in Nepal.
ref: Unit 1, Chapter 3: Celebrating Festivals

evidence: Festivals mark the seasons of farm work.
add: Add a survey: ask elders which festivals and foods come in each season; chart them.
point: Children can ask elders about festivals in each season and record the festivals and food in a chart.
ref: Unit 1, Chapter 3: Celebrating Festivals

evidence: A living thing that usually stays in one place, has green leaves
add: Add plants from tiny to tall, and leaf textures and smells; observe and describe the differences.
point: Plants vary widely in size, shape, leaf texture and smell, and observing them reveals their differences.
ref: Unit 2, Chapter 4: Getting to Know Plants

evidence: A tree trunk is a stem.
point: Trees have a trunk of wood, branches with leaves, and roots that go deep into the soil.
ref: Unit 2, Chapter 4: Getting to Know Plants

evidence: tell a tree from a shrub, a herb, a climber and a creeper by looking at their stem.
point: Shrubs are medium plants with several woody stems that grow close to the ground.
ref: Unit 2, Chapter 4: Getting to Know Plants

evidence: Doob grass, wheat, rice, sugarcane and bamboo are all grasses.
add: Add pulses (toor, moong, urad) come from shrubs; grains (rice, wheat, ragi) come from grasses.
point: Pulses like toor, moong and urad are seeds of shrubs, and grains like rice, wheat and ragi are seeds of grasses.
ref: Unit 2, Chapter 4: Getting to Know Plants

evidence: Most grasses have soft stems, so they are herbs.
add: Add grass leaves that are thin and flat and grass stems that are hollow, and sorting by stem and leaf.
point: Herbs have soft, non-woody stems, and grasses are a kind of herb with thin, flat leaves and hollow stems.
ref: Unit 2, Chapter 4: Getting to Know Plants

evidence: Why can a tree stand up alone, while a climber needs something to hold on to?
point: Climbers climb on other plants for support, while creepers spread along the ground, and some take food from their host.
ref: Unit 2, Chapter 4: Getting to Know Plants

evidence: Why can a tree stand up alone, while a climber needs something to hold on to?
add: Add grass as a sixth plant type, and a plant that is a climber with support but a creeper without.
point: Plants are grouped as tree, shrub, herb, grass, climber or creeper, and the same plant can behave differently with support.
ref: Unit 2, Chapter 4: Getting to Know Plants

evidence: I can write it in a results table.
add: Add keeping a plant friend: water and protect it, and record its leaves, flowers and fruit over weeks.
point: Caring for a plant means watering and protecting it, and recording its leaves, flowers and fruit over time.
ref: Unit 2, Chapter 4: Getting to Know Plants

evidence: A mango leaf, a tulsi leaf and a blade of grass are all leaves.
add: Add comparing leaves by colour, shape, texture and smell (tulsi, mint); draw and label them.
point: Leaves differ in colour, shape, size, texture and smell; some leaves like tulsi and mint have strong smells.
ref: Unit 2, Chapter 4: Getting to Know Plants

evidence: fat carrot-like roots storing food underground, a stem twining up a stick
point: Plants have roots, stems, leaves, flowers, fruits and seeds, and each part has a role.
ref: Unit 2, Chapter 4: Getting to Know Plants

evidence: Rub your hand on a tree trunk. The rough part you feel is bark.
add: Add bark rubbings and guessing trees by their bark pattern.
point: Bark is the hard outer covering of a tree trunk, and each tree has its own bark pattern.
ref: Unit 2, Chapter 4: Getting to Know Plants

evidence: Bamboo is a grass with a hard stem.
add: Add bamboo as the tallest grass, Rafflesia as the biggest flower, and sugar from sugarcane stems.
point: Plants are essential to life, and fun facts such as the tallest grass and the biggest flower show how varied they are.
ref: Unit 2, Chapter 4: Getting to Know Plants

evidence: A cut-away of soil with a tunnel and a rat curled up at the end.
add: Add animals living on, around and under plants, including in soil; children name the ones they know.
point: Where there are plants there are animals too, living on, around and under them.
ref: Unit 2, Chapter 5: Plants and Animals Live Together

evidence: a crow on a stick nest, pigeons on a ledge
add: Add how birds, squirrels and caterpillars use trees for food, nests and hiding, and ask why.
point: Animals such as birds, insects and squirrels use plants for food, nests, hiding and resting.
ref: Unit 2, Chapter 5: Plants and Animals Live Together

evidence: look at, feel and smell soil, shake it in a jar
point: Soil is the top layer of the earth made of broken rock, dead leaves, roots and living or dead animals.
ref: Unit 2, Chapter 5: Plants and Animals Live Together

evidence: how earthworms mix it all
add: Add soil after rain and away from plants, millipedes, and comparing soil samples from different places.
point: Soil changes after rain and away from plants, and wet soil shows earthworms and millipedes.
ref: Unit 2, Chapter 5: Plants and Animals Live Together

evidence: Earthworms live in damp soil.
add: Add soil creatures: ants, termites, beetles, grasshoppers; why some appear in the monsoon.
point: Many insects and creatures live in soil, some visible and some too small to see.
ref: Unit 2, Chapter 5: Plants and Animals Live Together

evidence: Count every animal you can see or hear.
point: Watching animals around a plant: count, describe and record what each animal is doing.
ref: Unit 2, Chapter 5: Plants and Animals Live Together

add: Add identifying birds by their calls, and how bird sounds change through the day.
point: Birds are identified by their calls, and the sounds change with time of day.
ref: Unit 2, Chapter 5: Plants and Animals Live Together

evidence: Carrot, radish, beetroot and shakarkand, which is sweet potato, are storage roots.
add: Add animals that use plant parts: camels eat leaves, bees drink nectar, owls nest in tree hollows.
point: Animals, birds and insects use plant parts: camels eat leaves, bees and butterflies drink nectar, bats rest on branches.
ref: Unit 2, Chapter 5: Plants and Animals Live Together

evidence: An egg on a curry leaf, a caterpillar, a chrysalis and a butterfly
point: The life of a caterpillar goes through changes: eating, forming a cocoon, emerging as a butterfly.
ref: Unit 2, Chapter 5: Plants and Animals Live Together

add: Add seeds and insects that wait for the rains and wake when they fall.
point: Living things depend on soil, and seeds and insects wait for the rains to appear.
ref: Unit 2, Chapter 5: Plants and Animals Live Together

evidence: small numbered circles drawn around a crow, an ant line, a pigeon
point: A plant friend is drawn with coloured dots to show where animals were spotted.
ref: Unit 2, Chapter 5: Plants and Animals Live Together

evidence: I can name ways to be kind to the small living things around me
point: We are connected to plants and animals, near our homes and far away, and should be kind to all living beings.
ref: Unit 2, Chapter 6: Living in Harmony

add: Add animals that come into our homes uninvited: how to respond with care, not harm.
point: Some animals and plants come into our homes uninvited, and we can respond with care or dislike.
ref: Unit 2, Chapter 6: Living in Harmony

evidence: Plants and animals need air, water and food too, and many need shelter.
point: Animals and plants that share our home need water, food and shelter from us.
ref: Unit 2, Chapter 6: Living in Harmony

evidence: Many fruits are sweet so that animals eat them and drop the seeds somewhere else.
point: A seed dropped by a monkey can grow into a new plant, showing how animals help plants.
ref: Unit 2, Chapter 6: Living in Harmony

evidence: I can name many ways people use plants: food, medicine, shade, wood, cloth, rope, paper and more.
point: We get food, medicine, fibre, wood, shade and fresh air from plants, and fruit from trees.
ref: Unit 2, Chapter 6: Living in Harmony

evidence: A cow grazing a green field beside a village tank
add: Add milk, curd and companionship from cows, buffaloes and goats, and why we respect them.
point: We get milk and company from cows, buffaloes and goats, so we respect and care for them.
ref: Unit 2, Chapter 6: Living in Harmony

add: Add two-way help: animal waste makes soil fertile and plants shelter animals (seed spreading is planned).
point: Animals help plants by spreading seeds and making soil fertile through their waste, while plants shelter and feed animals.
ref: Unit 2, Chapter 6: Living in Harmony

evidence: I can name the daily habits of at least three animals I have seen, such as when they wake, eat, rest and sleep.
add: Add one animal's movement, sounds and eating, shared as a short story with classmates.
point: A close look at one animal you see often: its name, movement, sounds, eating and behaviour.
ref: Unit 2, Chapter 6: Living in Harmony

evidence: An ant who finds sugar leaves a pheromone trail on her way home.
point: Ants find food by sense of smell, and different foods attract ants at different speeds.
ref: Unit 2, Chapter 6: Living in Harmony

add: NOT SCIENCE: befriending a tree and sharing feelings is emotional and social; belongs in a wellbeing or language unit.
point: Talking to a tree can help children express feelings and build empathy.
ref: Unit 2, Chapter 6: Living in Harmony

evidence: A hen and a crow both have feathers and two legs, but a hen and a cow do not.
point: Animals are grouped by number of legs: two, four, six and eight.
ref: Unit 2, Chapter 6: Living in Harmony

evidence: Each winter, a small grey bird called a curlew sandpiper lands on a mudflat
add: Add the Grey Wagtail visiting Valparai in winter, and children welcoming migrating birds with care.
point: The Grey Wagtail, a migratory bird, visits Valparai in winter, and children welcome it with posters and sweets.
ref: Unit 2, Chapter 6: Living in Harmony

evidence: Can today's sky tell you what tomorrow's weather will be?
point: Rain comes from clouds, and people guess whether rain will come using clues from the sky and elders.
ref: Unit 3, Chapter 7: Water - A Precious Gift

evidence: After a heavy shower, the water in the rain gauge was 12 mm deep.
add: Add observing raindrop size, speed and slant; sheets versus lines of rain.
point: Rain can be observed closely: its size, speed, heaviness and direction, and whether it looks like sheets or lines.
ref: Unit 3, Chapter 7: Water - A Precious Gift

evidence: Clear water is not always clean to drink. How can you tell?
point: Rainwater collected in a vessel can look clean or dirty, and may not be fit to drink.
ref: Unit 3, Chapter 7: Water - A Precious Gift

evidence: Water seeps into it from the sides and the bottom.
point: Rainwater goes into soil, collects in puddles or flows away, and some seeps underground.
ref: Unit 3, Chapter 7: Water - A Precious Gift

evidence: Rain is fresh water, yet the sea is salty.
point: Water flows from streams to rivers, and collects in ponds, lakes, seas and oceans.
ref: Unit 3, Chapter 7: Water - A Precious Gift

evidence: a borewell pipe reaching down
point: Water reaches homes through pipes, tanks on roofs, taps, wells, borewells, hand pumps and tankers.
ref: Unit 3, Chapter 7: Water - A Precious Gift

add: Add listing everyday water uses (brushing, bathing, cooking, cleaning) and estimating how much each takes.
point: Water is used for many daily activities, such as brushing teeth, bathing, cooking and cleaning.
ref: Unit 3, Chapter 7: Water - A Precious Gift

evidence: a clay matka cools water
add: Add copper, brass, steel and glass water vessels, and how families stored water long ago.
point: When water runs short, families store it in containers made of clay, copper, brass, steel, aluminium, glass or plastic.
ref: Unit 3, Chapter 7: Water - A Precious Gift

add: NOT SCIENCE: interviewing elders about old water vessels and writing a story is social and language work.
point: Elders recall how they got and stored water and what vessels they used, and this can become a story.
ref: Unit 3, Chapter 7: Water - A Precious Gift

evidence: I can sort used water by where it can go next: plants, mopping, flushing or the drain.
point: Water is used and then dirty; used water can be reused for plants or toilets but not for drinking or cooking.
ref: Unit 3, Chapter 7: Water - A Precious Gift

evidence: people built stepwells, so they could walk down to the water as it fell lower in summer.
point: Water is precious, and some places have little water, so everyone should get clean drinking water.
ref: Unit 3, Chapter 7: Water - A Precious Gift

add: Add a birdbath to water habitats: a shallow dish of clean water with stones, cleaned twice a week.
point: A birdbath is a shallow dish of fresh water with stones, cleaned twice a week, to help birds and insects.
ref: Unit 3, Chapter 7: Water - A Precious Gift

evidence: a heap of rice and a banana, with a small flame drawn above them for energy.
point: We eat and drink because food gives energy and strength, and we like different tastes.
ref: Unit 3, Chapter 8: Food We Eat

evidence: Why not just eat rice, or just eat sweets?
point: A balanced diet with many kinds of food keeps the body strong, and a champion athlete needs variety.
ref: Unit 3, Chapter 8: Food We Eat

evidence: Eating only rice and pickle for weeks is not balanced.
point: Food cooked at home is good, and too much of one food can leave the body weak.
ref: Unit 3, Chapter 8: Food We Eat

evidence: It holds sweet jaggery, sour tamarind, salt, bitter neem flowers, hot pepper
point: Chhappan bhog is a special offering of 56 food items, representing the six tastes: sweet, spicy, astringent, sour, salty, bitter.
ref: Unit 3, Chapter 8: Food We Eat

evidence: eating with the seasons
add: Add seasonal foods: mangoes and melons in summer, apples and soups in winter; compare the two.
point: Food comes from plants and animals, and foods are eaten in their seasons.
ref: Unit 3, Chapter 8: Food We Eat

evidence: Why do you sweat when you are hot and shiver when you are cold?
point: Our body loses water through sweat, so we must drink water and other drinks often in summer and when we play.
ref: Unit 3, Chapter 8: Food We Eat

evidence: which part of a plant a food comes from: root, stem, leaf, flower, fruit or seed.
point: Food is grown in fields as crops, and many foods come from plants in parts such as leaves, fruit, roots, stems, seeds.
ref: Unit 3, Chapter 8: Food We Eat

evidence: Curd comes from milk, milk comes from a cow, and a cow eats grass.
point: Foods also come from animals, such as milk, curd, ghee, paneer, honey, eggs and meat.
ref: Unit 3, Chapter 8: Food We Eat

evidence: a salt pan by the sea
point: Some ingredients come from neither plants nor animals, like salt.
ref: Unit 3, Chapter 8: Food We Eat

evidence: A glass of lassi: milk from a cow or buffalo, microbes that turned the milk into curd, sugar
point: Food that mixes plant and animal ingredients, such as lassi, is made of several sources.
ref: Unit 3, Chapter 8: Food We Eat

add: Add food waste: cook and serve only what is eaten, and compost leftovers. Sharing with guests is social.
point: Food should not be wasted, and sharing food with friends and guests is good.
ref: Unit 3, Chapter 8: Food We Eat

evidence: Five small heaps of different coloured dals on a steel plate.
add: Add regional dishes and home favourites; children compare what each place eats and why.
point: Food differs across regions, and children can find out about dishes from different places.
ref: Unit 3, Chapter 8: Food We Eat

evidence: Brush your teeth twice a day, morning and night.
point: Healthy habits keep bodies clean and free from disease, and they help minds work well too.
ref: Unit 3, Chapter 9: Staying Healthy and Happy

evidence: Brush your teeth twice a day, morning and night.
point: A daily routine includes brushing twice, washing hands with soap, drinking 6 to 8 glasses of water, eating, sleeping 8 hours, and playing outside.
ref: Unit 3, Chapter 9: Staying Healthy and Happy

evidence: I can wash my hands properly, for at least 20 seconds, at the moments that matter most
point: Hand washing with soap is needed after the toilet and after coming home from outdoors.
ref: Unit 3, Chapter 9: Staying Healthy and Happy

evidence: If you brush too hard, your gums can get sore.
add: Add datun: neem and babool twigs, how gums are cleaned, and how it compares with a toothbrush.
point: Traditional tooth cleaning used twigs such as neem and babool, the root of the modern toothbrush, called datun.
ref: Unit 3, Chapter 9: Staying Healthy and Happy

evidence: The reetha activity says to soak the shells at least 15 minutes beforehand
point: Traditional and natural cleaners, such as reetha and shikakai for hair, and a home cleaner from orange or lemon peels.
ref: Unit 3, Chapter 9: Staying Healthy and Happy

add: Add how monkeys groom each other and birds preen their feathers; compare with our own hygiene.
point: Animals keep themselves clean: monkeys groom each other, and birds use their beaks to clean feathers.
ref: Unit 3, Chapter 9: Staying Healthy and Happy

evidence: why moving makes you breathe hard
point: Exercise makes the heart work harder and better, and makes us breathe faster and sweat.
ref: Unit 3, Chapter 9: Staying Healthy and Happy

evidence: compare three kinds of exercise, move like a crab, frog and cat
point: Exercise has three types: strengthening the heart and lungs, building muscles and bones, and improving flexibility.
ref: Unit 3, Chapter 9: Staying Healthy and Happy

evidence: move like a crab, frog and cat
point: Fun actions and skipping games build fitness and can be done with friends.
ref: Unit 3, Chapter 9: Staying Healthy and Happy

evidence: How far your body can bend and stretch without pain.
add: Add staying active for mind and body: elders and people with pain can still play chess and walk.
point: Staying active helps both mind and body, and people with pain can still play games like chess.
ref: Unit 3, Chapter 9: Staying Healthy and Happy

evidence: find how steep a roof should be to shed rain
add: Add why busy roads, roofs without railings and construction sites are unsafe to play on; a park is safer.
point: Playing safely: a busy road, roof without railings and a construction site are unsafe places to play; a park or school ground is safer.
ref: Unit 3, Chapter 9: Staying Healthy and Happy

add: NOT SCIENCE: add a personal-safety role-play to the body-parts unit: say no to strangers and find a trusted adult.
point: Strangers can be unsafe, so children should not go with anyone they do not know, unless a trusted adult is with them.
ref: Unit 3, Chapter 9: Staying Healthy and Happy

evidence: A child squeezing a clothes peg at a table, a small timer beside her.
add: Add a weekly health table and a 24-hour clock to track sleep, meals, play and how each day feels.
point: A weekly health table and a 24-hour clock help track sleep, meals, play, and how each day feels.
ref: Unit 3, Chapter 9: Staying Healthy and Happy

evidence: which things people made
point: Things around us are made of materials that come from plants, animals, rocks or the earth, and people make others.
ref: Unit 4, Chapter 10: This World of Things

evidence: A child holding a steel tumbler, with thin dotted lines running from it back to a hill with a mine
add: Add metals from ore dug from the earth, and alloys (steel, brass, bronze) as mixtures of metals.
point: Metals such as iron, copper and gold come from ore dug from the earth; alloys like steel and brass are mixtures of metals.
ref: Unit 4, Chapter 10: This World of Things

evidence: Transparent, translucent and opaque: which things we can see through
point: Materials differ in how light passes through them: transparent, translucent and opaque.
ref: Unit 4, Chapter 10: This World of Things

evidence: let only one colour through a filter.
point: Looking through coloured transparent objects changes the colour of what we see.
ref: Unit 4, Chapter 10: This World of Things

evidence: A glass bangle is clear, but the sand it is made from is not.
point: Glass is made mostly from sand and is used for windowpanes and bulbs because it is transparent.
ref: Unit 4, Chapter 10: This World of Things

evidence: Breathe on a cold steel plate and it goes dull for a moment
point: Materials feel different: smooth, rough, dull, shiny or cold, and we can know them even with eyes closed.
ref: Unit 4, Chapter 10: This World of Things

evidence: A girl tapping a tabla
add: Add tapping wood, metal, plastic, cloth and glass to compare the ting and thak sounds.
point: Different materials make different sounds when tapped, and we can describe and compose beats with them.
ref: Unit 4, Chapter 10: This World of Things

evidence: test whether a material snaps or bends, how flexible it is
point: Flexible materials such as fabric suit clothes, while hard materials like wood suit tables.
ref: Unit 4, Chapter 10: This World of Things

evidence: Solids, liquids and gases: why water takes the shape of its glass
point: Solids keep their shape, liquids flow and take the shape of a container, and gases spread out and fill a space.
ref: Unit 4, Chapter 10: This World of Things

evidence: a clay diya
add: Add hard-to-classify materials: sand, sponge, clay, bees' wax versus artificial wax, and plastic waste.
point: Some materials, like sand, sponge and clay, are hard to classify, and some matter is made by people and some naturally.
ref: Unit 4, Chapter 10: This World of Things

evidence: I can tell natural things from things made by people
point: Natural things exist without people, such as trees, water and air, while artificial things are made by people, such as clothes and tables.
ref: Unit 4, Chapter 10: This World of Things

evidence: half with fresh light-green leaves and tiny white flowers
point: Trees flowering and fruiting at certain times of the year helps us to guess the season.
ref: Unit 4, Chapter 10: This World of Things

evidence: drop clay from different heights, catch a bouncing ball in a wet print
add: Add how a potter wets, kneads and shapes clay on a spinning wheel; clay neither too wet nor dry.
point: Clay from the earth is shaped into pots by a potter, who wets, kneads and spins it on a wheel.
ref: Unit 4, Chapter 11: Making Things

evidence: A row of three fires: a clay diya, a blue gas stove ring
add: Add why baking clay in a kiln hardens it, and how fire changes clay.
point: Pots are dried and then baked in a kiln, a hot oven, to make them hard and ready to use.
ref: Unit 4, Chapter 11: Making Things

evidence: a clay diya
add: Add: shaping a clay object by hand and decorating it with patterns; a clay piggy bank as a project.
point: Potters and families decorate pots with patterns, and children can help with colouring.
ref: Unit 4, Chapter 11: Making Things

evidence: watch it settle into layers
add: Add: sieve soil, settle it in water, pour off the water, shape the clay dough and sun-dry it.
point: Clay can be prepared at home: sieve soil, let it settle in water, and shape the dough into objects that dry in the sun.
ref: Unit 4, Chapter 11: Making Things

evidence: So do the stripes on a tiger.
point: Patterns repeat in nature, such as leaves, leopard spots, stripes on zebras and peacock feathers.
ref: Unit 4, Chapter 11: Making Things

evidence: Baking makes soft clay into hard pottery and bricks.
point: Bricks are shaped in moulds from mud, then baked in a kiln, and they build houses, schools and hospitals.
ref: Unit 4, Chapter 11: Making Things

evidence: safety rules for building sites and for homes
add: Add: helmet, safety vest and sturdy shoes on a building site, and why each one protects the worker.
point: Buildings are built brick by brick, and construction needs safety gear such as helmets, vests and sturdy shoes.
ref: Unit 4, Chapter 11: Making Things

evidence: houses made of mud, bamboo, stone and grass
point: Houses are built from different materials, such as mud, grass, wood and cow dung, depending on the climate.
ref: Unit 4, Chapter 11: Making Things

evidence: push-test both frames
point: Shape affects strength: stacking bricks in one arrangement can be sturdier than another.
ref: Unit 4, Chapter 11: Making Things

evidence: Ask 'What is it made of?' and you get the material.
add: Add: an interview with a craftsperson or elder on how a pencil or notebook is made.
point: Interviews with craftspeople and elders reveal how everyday objects like pencils and notebooks are made.
ref: Unit 4, Chapter 11: Making Things

evidence: batteries, tube lights, medicines and broken glass
point: Waste is made in daily life, from packaging, peels, paper and batteries, and it ends up in piles.
ref: Unit 4, Chapter 12: Taking Charge of Waste

evidence: Rain water caught in a thrown-away coconut shell
add: Add: why cows and other animals eat plastic, and why burning plastic releases harmful gases.
point: Waste harms animals, people and the air: animals eat plastic, burning plastic releases gases, and garbage breeds mosquitoes.
ref: Unit 4, Chapter 12: Taking Charge of Waste

evidence: why reducing comes first
point: Waste is managed by reducing it first, using cloth bags and avoiding packaged food.
ref: Unit 4, Chapter 12: Taking Charge of Waste

evidence: Old saris stitched together into a warm kantha quilt.
point: Reusing things instead of throwing them away, such as quilts from old sarees or refilling a steel bottle.
ref: Unit 4, Chapter 12: Taking Charge of Waste

evidence: The newspaper bag's bottom fold is hard
point: Old newspaper can be made into toys and bags, and newspaper or cloth can wrap gifts in an eco-friendly way.
ref: Unit 4, Chapter 12: Taking Charge of Waste

evidence: Handmade Recycled Paper, and a Thank-you Card
point: Waste can be made into a gift to thank people who keep the home or locality clean.
ref: Unit 4, Chapter 12: Taking Charge of Waste

evidence: Bengaluru and Indore ask every home to hand over waste sorted.
add: Add: a village example such as Silluk and what local people did to become zero-waste.
point: Some villages are clean because of local action, such as Silluk, a zero-waste village in Arunachal Pradesh.
ref: Unit 4, Chapter 12: Taking Charge of Waste

evidence: Many cities use a green bin for wet waste and a blue bin for dry waste.
point: Waste is sorted into a green dustbin for wet, rotting waste that becomes compost, and a blue dustbin for recyclable metal, glass, plastic and paper.
ref: Unit 4, Chapter 12: Taking Charge of Waste

evidence: say how to keep it safe for the people
add: Add: wrap sharp glass and needles in cloth and paper to protect sanitation workers.
point: Sharp things such as broken glass and needles should be wrapped in cloth and paper to protect sanitation workers.
ref: Unit 4, Chapter 12: Taking Charge of Waste

evidence: A tidy street with a covered drain
add: Add: tidying the home, using brooms, and the national cleanliness pledge on Cleanliness Day.
point: Keeping home and school clean involves tidying up, using tools such as brooms, and being responsible for waste.
ref: Unit 4, Chapter 12: Taking Charge of Waste

evidence: instead of a thin carry bag
add: Add: replacing plastic with cloth or steel, and planning a zero-waste party.
point: Plastic can be replaced with safer materials, and a zero-waste party reduces waste.
ref: Unit 4, Chapter 12: Taking Charge of Waste

evidence: A family is a group of people who look after each other.
point: A family is the smallest unit of society, usually a couple and their unmarried children, sometimes with several generations.
ref: Lesson 1: Concept of Family and Interpersonal Relations

evidence: A joint family is a big family where grandparents, parents, uncles, aunts and cousins live together.
point: There are two kinds of family: joint families, where several generations share one home, and nuclear families of parents and children.
ref: Lesson 1: Concept of Family and Interpersonal Relations

add: NOT SCIENCE: add how joint and nuclear families share costs and decisions, and the help each gives, to family unit.
point: Joint families share costs and property under a head's decisions, while nuclear families decide together but lack help at short notice.
ref: Lesson 1: Concept of Family and Interpersonal Relations

evidence: Parents also give time: talking, listening and helping a child to decide things.
add: NOT SCIENCE: add respect, shared responsibility and settling family quarrels by talking, to family unit.
point: Family bonds stay strong when members respect and help each other, avoid hurting feelings, and settle differences by talking.
ref: Lesson 1: Concept of Family and Interpersonal Relations

add: NOT SCIENCE: add parents' role in raising children: praise over harsh punishment, values and children copying parents, to family unit.
point: Parents must help children grow healthy, educated, talented, well-mannered and responsible, and they should praise rather than harshly punish.
ref: Lesson 1: Concept of Family and Interpersonal Relations

evidence: The law also bans most paid work for children under 14.
add: NOT SCIENCE: add children's health care, vaccination, food, and time to study and play; child-labour ban already in family unit.
point: Children need regular health care, vaccination, proper food, clothes suited to them, and time to study and play rather than earn wages.
ref: Lesson 1: Concept of Family and Interpersonal Relations

evidence: how girls and women were kept out of school
add: NOT SCIENCE: add female infanticide, feticide, dowry and unequal diet and play to the girls-and-women card in family unit.
point: Girls face lower status than boys from birth through practices such as female infanticide, feticide and dowry, and through unequal diet, schooling and play.
ref: Lesson 1: Concept of Family and Interpersonal Relations

evidence: India's Constitution gives women and men equal rights.
add: NOT SCIENCE: add women's property, maintenance, equal pay, domestic-violence protection and 33 per cent reserved Panchayat seats.
point: Laws and schemes support women: equal property rights, maintenance after divorce, equal pay, protection from domestic violence and reserved local seats.
ref: Lesson 1: Concept of Family and Interpersonal Relations

evidence: Girls and women, then and now
add: NOT SCIENCE: add women's present roles (teachers, doctors, sarpanch) and the gap that remains, with laws not enforced, to family unit.
point: Women now work as teachers, nurses, doctors and sarpanch, yet many still lack property rights, face violence and are not treated equally.
ref: Lesson 1: Concept of Family and Interpersonal Relations

add: NOT SCIENCE: add how families and government care for elders: food, safety, pensions, maintenance rights, reserved seats.
point: Elders anchor a family, so family and society must care for them with food, safety and respect, and government offers them support.
ref: Lesson 1: Concept of Family and Interpersonal Relations

evidence: Hand signs, or sign language: no sound needed.
add: NOT SCIENCE: add disability dignity, Braille, special schools and reserved jobs; sign language touched in transport-and-communication.
point: People with disabilities, including children, deserve dignity, so we never mock them, and society offers special schools, sign language and Braille.
ref: Lesson 1: Concept of Family and Interpersonal Relations

evidence: The cobbler, who mends shoes and chappals.
point: Neighbourhood workers such as barbers, washermen, cobblers, potters, weavers, blacksmiths and carpenters each meet a daily need.
ref: Lesson 2: Our Social Environment

evidence: A nurse and a tailor both have professions
add: NOT SCIENCE: add how trades change over time with machines, training, growing families and moves to towns, to community-and-helpers.
point: Professions change over time as families grow, children learn new skills, machines arrive and people move to towns for work.
ref: Lesson 2: Our Social Environment

evidence: A group of people who live near each other, share places and things, and depend on each other.
point: No profession is small or big, because every person depends on others, so respecting and cooperating with every worker keeps life running.
ref: Lesson 2: Our Social Environment

evidence: I can say what public services such as a government school, a health centre, the post office
point: Public services such as hospitals, schools, banks, post offices and police are either government or non-government, and they make daily life smoother.
ref: Lesson 2: Our Social Environment

evidence: free vaccines at the government health centre
add: NOT SCIENCE: add government and private hospitals, emergency priority and the free ambulance for poor patients to community-and-helpers.
point: Hospitals treat patients and vaccinate children, offering free general-ward care, emergency priority and a free ambulance for poor patients.
ref: Lesson 2: Our Social Environment

evidence: Private schools must keep a quarter of the seats in the first class of the school for children from poor families
point: Schools must teach children up to class 8 without fees, provide free books and meals, and reserve private-school seats for poor children.
ref: Lesson 2: Our Social Environment

evidence: PIN stands for Postal Index Number
add: NOT SCIENCE: add what the post office does (letters, parcels, money orders, savings, MGNREGA deposits) and private couriers, to transport-and-communication.
point: The post office delivers letters, parcels and money orders, takes savings deposits and teaches small savings schemes, while private couriers also deliver.
ref: Lesson 2: Our Social Environment

add: NOT SCIENCE: add what banks do: safe keeping, interest on deposits, loans for farming and business; planned in community-and-helpers.L4 but not yet written.
point: Banks keep money and valuables safe, pay interest on deposits, and lend at lower interest for farming, education and business.
ref: Lesson 2: Our Social Environment

evidence: Traffic police at night wear jackets with reflective stripes.
add: NOT SCIENCE: add police work: FIR, investigation, arrest, keeping peace, to community-and-helpers.
point: The police protect people, guard traffic, register FIRs, investigate crimes and keep peace, law and order in society.
ref: Lesson 2: Our Social Environment

evidence: if an office refuses it, a person can complain or go to court
add: NOT SCIENCE: add the court ladder from Gram Panchayat to the Supreme Court and free legal aid, to india.government-and-rights.
point: Village disputes go first to the Panchayat, then to courts: district court, High Court and the Supreme Court, which has the final word.
ref: Lesson 2: Our Social Environment

evidence: on the municipality for water
add: NOT SCIENCE: add what Gram Panchayats and municipalities each provide: roads, cleaning, electricity, birth and death registration, to community-and-helpers.
point: Municipal bodies and village Panchayats provide water, roads, cleaning, electricity, birth and death registration and village development.
ref: Lesson 2: Our Social Environment

add: NOT SCIENCE: add cooperating with public-service workers, not obstructing doctors, nurses or sanitation staff, to community-and-helpers.
point: Respecting public-service workers means cooperating with them and not obstructing their work, such as fighting with doctors or nurses.
ref: Lesson 2: Our Social Environment

evidence: One harvest festival in January has different names across India
add: NOT SCIENCE: add that festivals share messages of brotherhood, love and good over evil, not only harvest timing, to festivals.
point: Festivals across India, whatever the religion or region, carry messages of brotherhood, love, humanity and good over evil, and many follow harvest and seasons.
ref: Lesson 3: Our Festivals

evidence: I can say what Independence Day, Republic Day and Gandhi Jayanti remember, with their dates.
point: Three national festivals are celebrated by everyone: Independence Day, Republic Day and Gandhi Jayanti.
ref: Lesson 3: Our Festivals

evidence: one harvest festival in January has different names across India, such as Pongal, Makara Sankranti
point: Makar Sankranti in January, when the sun enters Makar Rashi, is a harvest festival with many regional names and foods.
ref: Lesson 3: Our Festivals

evidence: Holi colours were once made from flowers, such as the orange flowers of the palash tree
point: Holi welcomes spring; the Holika legend shows good defeating evil, and the festival stresses colour, music and forgiving old quarrels.
ref: Lesson 3: Our Festivals

evidence: Eid-ul-Fitr ends a month of fasting and is a time to give to people in need.
point: Eid-ul-Fitr ends the month of Ramazan fasting after the moon is sighted, with prayer, charity, new clothes, sweets and gifts of Eidi.
ref: Lesson 3: Our Festivals

evidence: Guru Nanak Jayanti
add: NOT SCIENCE: add Guru Nanak Jayanti: birth of the first Sikh Guru, and langar serving everyone equally, to festivals.
point: Guru Nanak Jayanti, also called Prakash Utsav, marks the birth of the first Sikh Guru, and langar serves everyone regardless of caste or status.
ref: Lesson 3: Our Festivals

evidence: At the Mysuru Dasara exhibition
add: NOT SCIENCE: add Dussehra's victory of good over evil: Navratri fasts, Ramlila and burning of Ravana effigies, to festivals.
point: Dussehra and Durga Puja celebrate victory of good over evil through Navratri fasts, Ramlila plays and burning of Ravana, Kumbhkaran and Meghnad effigies.
ref: Lesson 3: Our Festivals

evidence: Diwali falls on a new moon night
add: NOT SCIENCE: add Deepawali's stories (light over darkness, Rama's return) and the harm from fireworks, linked to pollution and sound units.
point: Deepawali celebrates light over darkness and Rama's return to Ayodhya over five days, but noisy fireworks and gambling harm air, sound and health.
ref: Lesson 3: Our Festivals

evidence: At Christmas, homes in Kerala hang paper star lanterns.
add: NOT SCIENCE: add Christmas's meaning: Jesus's birth and his message of love and service to the poor, to festivals.
point: Christmas on 25 December marks Jesus Christ's birth and his message of love and service to the poor, shared through church, feasts and gifts.
ref: Lesson 3: Our Festivals

evidence: Buddha Purnima falls on a full moon day in April or May.
add: NOT SCIENCE: add Mahavir Jayanti and Buddha's compassion as shared values of non-violence, to festivals.
point: Mahavir Jayanti and Buddha Purnima honour the non-violence of Lord Mahavira and the compassion of Lord Buddha, showing shared values.
ref: Lesson 3: Our Festivals

add: NOT SCIENCE: add how festivals stay clean and kind: avoid smoking, chewing tobacco or drinking, and clean the neighbourhood on festival days.
point: Festivals can be kept clean and kind by avoiding harmful habits such as smoking, chewing tobacco or drinking, and by cleaning the neighbourhood.
ref: Lesson 3: Our Festivals

evidence: I can say what the environment is, and name living and non-living parts of the environment around my home.
point: The environment is everything around us: people, buildings, animals, plants, water, air, soil and the social and political surroundings.
ref: Lesson 4: The Environment

evidence: I can compare a pond, a forest, a desert and the sea
add: Add mountain and plains environments with pine, yak, and crops; planned lands-and-lives.L4 can carry the detail.
point: Each place has its own environment: villages, cities, forests, deserts, mountains, plains and sea-shores differ in land, plants and animals.
ref: Lesson 4: The Environment

evidence: I can say what the environment is, and name living and non-living parts of the environment around my home.
point: The environment divides into physical parts, which we sense without life, and biological parts, which are living.
ref: Lesson 4: The Environment

evidence: When a living thing dies, the mending stops
point: Living things show signs of life: they eat, breathe, grow, make young like themselves, feel, and die after a limited life.
ref: Lesson 4: The Environment

evidence: A cat is alive. A stone is not.
point: Comparing a cat with a bicycle is a test: the cat shows life signs and the bicycle none, so the signs decide what is living.
ref: Lesson 4: The Environment

evidence: A huge tree grows from a small seed, yet the soil it grows in hardly gets lighter.
point: Plants are living: they make their own food from air and water, breathe, grow, produce seeds, and their flowers open and close.
ref: Lesson 4: The Environment

evidence: A river, a rock, a cloud, a coconut and a neem tree are natural.
point: Natural things are made by nature, such as the sun and rivers; man-made things come from human wisdom and labour, such as roads.
ref: Lesson 4: The Environment

evidence: I can sort plants into trees, shrubs, herbs, climbers and creepers
add: Add: identify plants by leaves, flowers and fruit (neem, tulsi, rose); animals by how they move: fly, swim, walk, hop, crawl.
point: Common plants and animals are identified by size, shape, leaves, flowers, fruit, body features, how they move and where they live.
ref: Lesson 4: The Environment

evidence: A Kangayam bullock that pulls a cart in Tamil Nadu is a domestic animal.
add: Add: bullocks plough, donkeys and camels carry loads, bees give honey, silkworms give silk, dogs guard homes.
point: Animals have long helped people: bullocks plough, donkeys and camels carry loads, cows and goats give milk, bees give honey and worms enrich soil.
ref: Lesson 5: Conservation of Environment

evidence: Pet dogs get a rabies vaccine every year
add: Add: clean airy shelter, nutritious food, medical care, and no caged birds or circus cruelty.
point: Caring for animals means clean, airy shelter, nutritious food, vaccination against rabies, medical care and no cruelty in circuses or caged birds.
ref: Lesson 5: Conservation of Environment

evidence: It holds the plant in the soil and soaks up water.
point: Each plant part has a job: roots take in water, stems carry it, leaves make food, and flowers and fruit hold seeds.
ref: Lesson 5: Conservation of Environment

evidence: green leaves make sugar from sunlight, water and carbon dioxide, and give out oxygen
point: Leaves are the plant's kitchen: with sunlight they make food from water and carbon dioxide, releasing oxygen; plants also give grains and wood.
ref: Lesson 5: Conservation of Environment

evidence: Each of them is part of a long line of eating that starts with sunlight on a leaf.
point: Energy moves along food chains: plants are eaten by plant-eaters, which are eaten by meat-eaters, and scavengers and decomposers recycle the rest.
ref: Lesson 5: Conservation of Environment

evidence: Grass, then grasshopper, then frog, then snake, then eagle.
add: Add: what happens when one link is removed: losing frogs lets insects multiply; losing lions lets deer damage fields.
point: Removing one link upsets the whole chain: losing frogs lets insects and mosquitoes multiply, and losing lions lets deer damage fields.
ref: Lesson 5: Conservation of Environment

evidence: Soap, oil, paint and factory waste make water harmful too.
add: Add: chemical fertilisers and pesticides that kill useful worms and bees, and the soil they pollute.
point: Factory waste, chemical fertilisers and smoke from factories and vehicles pollute water, soil and air, kill useful organisms and cause diseases.
ref: Lesson 5: Conservation of Environment

evidence: why a bare field loses its soil in the rain
point: Topsoil took a very long time to form; grass and forests protect it, while cutting trees and overgrazing let wind and water wash it away.
ref: Lesson 5: Conservation of Environment

evidence: test whether a mat of roots holds soil in water
add: Add: forests clean the air, cool the land, slow rain to prevent floods and droughts, and give useful products.
point: Forests clean the air, cool the surroundings, hold soil with roots, slow rainwater to prevent floods and droughts, and supply many useful products.
ref: Lesson 5: Conservation of Environment

evidence: Planting trees on a hillside, so their roots hold the soil.
add: Add: reporting polluters, cutting chemical use, and organic farming as everyday environment habits.
point: Simple habits protect the environment: plant trees, keep surroundings clean, compost waste, cut chemicals, avoid plastic and report polluters.
ref: Lesson 5: Conservation of Environment

evidence: I can explain why rain is fresh even though the sea is salty
point: Rain seeps into the ground and fills rivers that reach the sea, where water is salty and unfit for drinking or farming.
ref: Lesson 5: Conservation of Environment

evidence: a tank on the roof
add: Add: reuse used water for plants, and harvest rain from roofs into tanks.
point: Save water at home: do not waste it, reuse dirty water for plants, keep water bodies clean, and harvest rain from roofs into tanks.
ref: Lesson 5: Conservation of Environment

evidence: I can say what makes something a planet
point: The Sun, Earth, Moon, planets, satellites and stars together make up the solar system, and the Sun is the star at its centre.
ref: Lesson 6: Sun-Moon-Stars, Day-Night and Seasons

evidence: Sun, Moon and stars: why the Sun is a star and the Moon is not
point: Stars make their own light, while planets such as Earth receive their light from a star, so Earth is a planet.
ref: Lesson 6: Sun-Moon-Stars, Day-Night and Seasons

evidence: why Pluto is now called a dwarf planet
point: There are eight planets around the Sun: Mercury, Venus, Earth, Mars, Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus and Neptune; Pluto is now doubted as a planet.
ref: Lesson 6: Sun-Moon-Stars, Day-Night and Seasons

evidence: most planets have moons
add: DATED: moon counts keep changing; keep the idea and examples, such as Jupiter's four big moons, not the numbers.
point: Satellites circle planets: the Moon circles Earth, and the book gives satellite counts for Mars, Saturn, Jupiter, Uranus and Neptune.
ref: Lesson 6: Sun-Moon-Stars, Day-Night and Seasons

evidence: how Indian calendars count the Moon's days, the tithis and the pakshas
point: The Moon's shape changes over about fifteen days from new Amavasya to full Poornima, and two fortnights, Krishna and Shukla Paksha, guide Indian calendars.
ref: Lesson 6: Sun-Moon-Stars, Day-Night and Seasons

evidence: Day and night happen because the Earth spins.
point: The Earth spins on its tilted axis about once every 24 hours, so the Sun-facing side has day and the other side has night.
ref: Lesson 6: Sun-Moon-Stars, Day-Night and Seasons

evidence: Everyone agrees that the tilt of the Earth sets this yearly rhythm.
add: Board says distance from the Sun causes seasons; that is wrong. Keep the unit's tilt explanation.
point: The Earth orbits the Sun in about 365 days, and its changing distance from the Sun changes heat and so brings the seasons.
ref: Lesson 6: Sun-Moon-Stars, Day-Night and Seasons

add: Add to sky.history-of-astronomy: weekday names from the Sun, Moon and planets (Ravivar, Somvar).
point: Some weekday names come from the sky: Sunday is Ravivar after Ravi, the Sun, and Monday is Somvar after Som, the Moon.
ref: Lesson 6: Sun-Moon-Stars, Day-Night and Seasons

evidence: Science vs stories that only sound true.
point: Folk stories about Earth on a cow's horn, grandparents as stars or the Moon as uncle are not science; evidence gives the true account.
ref: Lesson 6: Sun-Moon-Stars, Day-Night and Seasons

evidence: The seven stars of the Saptarishi look like a ladle.
point: The Pole Star stays fixed in the north, near the seven-star Saptarishi (Ursa Major) group; the Milky Way and comets are seen too.
ref: Lesson 6: Sun-Moon-Stars, Day-Night and Seasons

evidence: In Delhi, the longest day in June has about 14 hours of daylight
add: Add: observing equal day and night at the equinox, with the Pole Star's place, as a sky-watching task.
point: Observe the sky and day length: when day and night are equal, when days are longest and shortest, and where the Pole Star appears.
ref: Lesson 6: Sun-Moon-Stars, Day-Night and Seasons

evidence: I can name the five basic needs, and say which three we cannot live without at all, and why.
point: Air, water and food are needed to survive; clothing and shelter are also basic needs that protect the body and support daily life.
ref: Lesson 7: Our Basic Needs

evidence: how oxygen reaches every part of you
point: We breathe in oxygen from air, blood carries it to every part of the body, and we breathe out carbon dioxide.
ref: Lesson 7: Our Basic Needs

evidence: A tulsi plant on a sunny window is photosynthesising all day.
add: Add: keep homes airy, do not sleep in airtight rooms, and prevent pollution; trees add oxygen.
point: Keep air clean by ventilating homes, not sleeping in airtight rooms, preventing pollution and planting trees.
ref: Lesson 7: Our Basic Needs

evidence: Dehydration means your body has lost more water than you have drunk.
add: Add: water is about two-thirds of the body; urine and sweat carry waste out; 8 to 10 glasses a day.
point: Water is about two-thirds of the body, carries waste out as urine and sweat, and we should drink eight to ten glasses a day.
ref: Lesson 7: Our Basic Needs

evidence: how washing, covering, cooking and cooling each help keep food safe
point: Food supplies energy for work and thought; eat a balanced diet and cook hygienically, washing vegetables before cutting and avoiding stale food.
ref: Lesson 7: Our Basic Needs

evidence: why a sweater, a clay pot and a flask work, using the ideas of trapped air
add: Add: cotton keeps us cool, wool traps warm air, and silk and polyester compared; polyester is a plastic.
point: Clothes protect from cold, heat and wind; cotton keeps us cool, wool traps warm air, and silk and polyester are also common.
ref: Lesson 7: Our Basic Needs

evidence: find out how steep a roof should be to shed rain
point: Shelter protects us from rain, heat, cold, storms, snow and animals, and houses are built to suit the climate and the risks of each place.
ref: Lesson 7: Our Basic Needs

evidence: The part of food the body uses to build and repair itself, such as new skin and muscle.
point: Food gives energy for movement and thought, supports the growth and repair of the body, and builds resistance to disease.
ref: Lesson 8: Food

evidence: Carbohydrates: the body's main fuel
point: Carbohydrates and fats mainly give energy, while proteins help the body grow and repair itself.
ref: Lesson 8: Food

evidence: A nutrient the body needs in very small amounts to stay healthy.
point: Minerals and vitamins are needed only in small amounts, but they keep the body working and protect it from disease.
ref: Lesson 8: Food

evidence: sort foods into energy foods, body-building foods and protecting foods
point: A balanced diet has all five components in the right amounts, such as grains, pulses, vegetables, seasonal fruit and ghee or oil.
ref: Lesson 8: Food

evidence: India adds iodine to most salt, which has greatly reduced goitre
add: Add: name marasmus from too little food, anaemia from low iron, and goitre from low iodine as deficiency diseases.
point: Deficiencies cause disease: marasmus in small children from too little food, anaemia from low iron or vitamin B, and goitre from low iodine.
ref: Lesson 8: Food

evidence: Vitamin A helps your eyes see in dim light.
point: Vitamins A, C and D and calcium guard different body parts: A for eyes, C for gums and resistance, D and calcium for bones.
ref: Lesson 8: Food

evidence: Oral rehydration solution, ORS, has both salt and sugar dissolved in the same water.
point: Water is part of food too; vomiting and diarrhoea drain it, so doctors advise ORS, lemonade, soups or a salt-sugar drink.
ref: Lesson 8: Food

evidence: A glass of clear well water can carry germs that cause diarrhoea.
point: Dirty drinking water spreads jaundice, typhoid, cholera and diarrhoea, so water sources must be kept clean and covered.
ref: Lesson 8: Food

evidence: name ways to make water safe: settling, filtering, boiling and chlorine.
point: Dirty water can be cleaned with alum, a home filter of gravel, sand and charcoal, chlorine tablets, potassium permanganate, boiling, or ISI-marked filters.
ref: Lesson 8: Food

evidence: find out how many washes clean coriander
point: Keep cooking and eating clean: wash and soak grains and pulses, wash produce before cutting, cover food, wash hands and do not talk while eating.
ref: Lesson 8: Food

evidence: Write down their answers.
add: Add: a week's food diary, checked against the five food components, with a plan to change an unbalanced diet.
point: Keep a week's food diary, check whether the meals were balanced, and change the diet if it was not.
ref: Lesson 8: Food

evidence: I can name the external organs (skin, hair, nails, eyes, ears, nose, mouth and teeth, hands, feet and private parts)
point: External organs sit on or near the surface: in the head (hair, eyes, ears, nose, teeth), in the trunk (hands, legs), and skin.
ref: Lesson 9: Care and cleanliness of external organs

evidence: say the job of each one
point: Each external organ does its own job with the others: eyes see, ears hear, nose smells, teeth chew, hands work and skin protects.
ref: Lesson 9: Care and cleanliness of external organs

evidence: I can say how to care for each outer part of my body
point: Health depends on hygiene, diet and lifestyle, and people who care for every organ stay healthy and alert into old age.
ref: Lesson 9: Care and cleanliness of external organs

evidence: Many families still soak reetha and shikakai to wash hair.
add: Add: wash hair about twice a week with a mild cleanser, comb daily, and keep dirt out to prevent dandruff.
point: Wash hair about twice a week with a mild cleanser, comb daily, and keep dirt out, since dirt brings lice and dandruff.
ref: Lesson 9: Care and cleanliness of external organs

evidence: When smoke gets in your eyes, they fill with tears.
add: Add: wash eyes with clean water, never rub them, and take no eye medicine without a doctor.
point: Eyes should be washed with clean water and protected from dirt, smoke and bright light; never rub them or use medicine without a doctor.
ref: Lesson 9: Care and cleanliness of external organs

evidence: why nothing should go into the ear canal, and what earwax does
point: Never clean ears with straws, matchsticks or pins; keep water out and see a doctor for pain, discharge or a stuck object.
ref: Lesson 9: Care and cleanliness of external organs

evidence: To care for your nose, blow it gently into a handkerchief or tissue
add: Add: no tobacco, gutka or paan, and the harm they do to teeth and gums; rinse after meals.
point: Nose and mouth need care: a clean handkerchief for sneezing, brushing twice a day, rinsing after meals, and no tobacco, gutka or paan.
ref: Lesson 9: Care and cleanliness of external organs

evidence: some worm larvae in dirty soil can get in through bare feet.
point: Hands and feet carry germs: wash with soap before eating and after the toilet, clean hands before cooking, remove shoes indoors and trim nails.
ref: Lesson 9: Care and cleanliness of external organs

evidence: I know the correct names of my private parts and how to keep them clean.
add: Add: menstruation hygiene: a clean dry cloth or pad, changed and washed, and clean water after the toilet.
point: Private parts need clean water after the toilet, a clean dry cloth after urinating, and clean cloth or pads during menstruation.
ref: Lesson 9: Care and cleanliness of external organs

evidence: check whether your skin flakes off with sticky tape
add: Add: skin guards against heat, cold and dirt and lets out sweat; bathe daily, dry well, oil in winter, avoid harsh scrubs.
point: Skin guards against heat, cold and dirt and lets out sweat; bathe daily, dry well, oil in winter, and avoid harsh scrubs.
ref: Lesson 9: Care and cleanliness of external organs

evidence: The habits that keep our bodies, food, water and homes clean
add: Add: a ten-question yes/no hygiene self-check, with one habit to build for each 'no' answer.
point: Score yourself on ten yes/no hygiene habits, such as brushing, rinsing and combing, and build a habit for each 'no' answer.
ref: Lesson 9: Care and cleanliness of external organs

evidence: These things came by truck, train or ship, and then by a shop's van or a delivery scooter.
point: Transport lets people travel to school, work and relatives, and carries goods such as milk, fruit, vegetables and food products across regions.
ref: Lesson 10: Transport and Communication

evidence: how transport grew, from walking and boats to wheels, trains, ships and aeroplanes
point: Transport developed in stages: footpaths formed by footprints, then river travel and the wheel, which gave rise to road, rail, air and water transport.
ref: Lesson 10: Transport and Communication

evidence: A bullock cart has two big wooden wheels joined by one axle.
add: Add: the Grand Trunk Road and national highways, built by Sher Shah Suri; rural roads that connect villages.
point: Road transport includes cycles, rickshaws, buses, trucks, cars, bullock carts and tongas, and the Grand Trunk Road and national highways link places.
ref: Lesson 10: Transport and Communication

evidence: By the end I can read common road signs and traffic lights, and say what their shapes and colours mean.
point: Road signs warn of hazards such as bridges, schools and U-turns, or control traffic; red means stop, yellow means wait and see, green means go.
ref: Lesson 10: Transport and Communication

add: NOT SCIENCE: add India's railways: broad, metre and narrow gauges, and the first train Mumbai to Thane in 1853; check dates.
point: Indian railways use broad, metre and narrow gauge tracks; the first train ran from Mumbai to Thane in 1853, and metros and monorails are growing.
ref: Lesson 10: Transport and Communication

evidence: ferries carry people and bicycles across the wide Brahmaputra river
add: Add early water transport: fishing boats, then trade ships between countries; Ganga and Hooghly routes.
point: Water transport began with fishing boats, then ships carried trade between countries; the Ganga, Brahmaputra and Hooghly carry goods and people.
ref: Lesson 10: Transport and Communication

evidence: By helicopter
add: Add that air travel is fastest, reaching remote places such as Itanagar and Tawang by plane or helicopter.
point: Air transport is the fastest mode, reaching major cities, state capitals and remote places such as Itanagar and Tawang by aeroplane and helicopter.
ref: Lesson 10: Transport and Communication

evidence: such as water, petrol or cooking gas
point: Pipelines carry water, oil, natural gas, cooking gas, petrol and CNG, so liquids and gases reach homes without tankers.
ref: Lesson 10: Transport and Communication

evidence: Writing let a message travel without the person
add: Add block printing (China), letterpress and computer typesetting as steps in communication history.
point: Communication grew from drums, fire, smoke, mirrors and messengers, through trained pigeons, to letters, block printing, letterpress and computer typesetting.
ref: Lesson 10: Transport and Communication

evidence: the telegraph came in the 1800s, before the telephone in 1876
add: Add Indian dates: postal service 1837, telegraph 1860, radio 1920, Doordarshan 1959.
point: Indian milestones: postal service from 1837, telegraph linking cities by 1860, telephone 1876, radio broadcasting from 1920 and Delhi Doordarshan from 1959.
ref: Lesson 10: Transport and Communication

evidence: by talking, signs, writing, phones, radio, TV or the internet
add: Add teletext, SMS, fax and mandi price information; compare two modern tools and their advantages.
point: Modern tools such as TV, teletext, computers, email, SMS, fax, video calls and the internet share news, views and entertainment worldwide.
ref: Lesson 10: Transport and Communication

evidence: Ants leave a trail of smell from food to the nest
point: People also communicate without words through gestures, facial expressions, signs and symbols, drawings, and animal sounds and smells.
ref: Lesson 10: Transport and Communication

evidence: A few things are shared by all of them
point: India's diversity of religions, languages, dress, food and festivals is held together by shared national symbols that express unity and equality.
ref: Lesson 11: National Identity

evidence: White stands for peace and truth. Green stands for the land, growth and plenty
add: Give the board meanings: saffron for sacrifice, green for faith, wheel for progress; unit says green is land.
point: The flag is a 3:2 tricolour: saffron for sacrifice, white for peace and truth, green for faith, and a blue wheel for progress.
ref: Lesson 11: National Identity

evidence: Saffron is always on top
add: Add the rules: never print the flag on cloth or clothing; put nothing above or on it.
point: Respect the flag: keep it clean, never fly it torn or upside down, put nothing above or on it, and use half-mast for mourning.
ref: Lesson 11: National Identity

evidence: It comes from an old text called the Mundaka Upanishad
point: The national emblem, from the Sarnath Ashoka pillar, shows lions and the motto 'Satyamev Jayate' from the Mundaka Upanishad.
ref: Lesson 11: National Identity

evidence: Hunting them is a crime in India
add: Add that killing a peacock is punishable, and that the tiger stands for courage.
