point: The national animal is the tiger, a symbol of courage whose hunting is a crime; the national bird is the protected peacock.
ref: Lesson 11: National Identity

evidence: A flag, a tiger, a peacock and a lotus arranged in a circle
add: Explain the lotus staying clean in mud, and say why hockey is the national game in the board's sense.
point: The national flower is the lotus, which stays pure in mud, and the national game is hockey, which Indian players have won abroad.
ref: Lesson 11: National Identity

evidence: The full anthem takes about 52 seconds to sing
point: The national anthem, 'Jana-gana-mana', written by Rabindranath Tagore, is sung on national occasions, and it takes about 52 seconds to sing.
ref: Lesson 11: National Identity

evidence: Freedom fighters sang it at their marches
point: The national song 'Vande Mataram', by Bankim Chandra, built patriotism in the freedom movement and praises the motherland's fields, rivers and people.
ref: Lesson 11: National Identity

evidence: Gandhi Jayanti on 2 October is the birthday of Mahatma Gandhi
point: National days are 15 August (Independence Day, 1947), 26 January (Republic Day, when the Constitution came into effect) and 2 October (Gandhi Jayanti).
ref: Lesson 11: National Identity

evidence: Globalisation means the countries of the world becoming more connected through trade, travel
point: Globalization connects countries through transport, communication, trade and culture, changing lifestyles, food habits and customs.
ref: Lesson 12: Our Social and Economic Environment

evidence: Every child aged 6 to 14 in India has the right to a free school place.
point: The Right to Education Act 2009 guarantees free, compulsory education up to class 8 for children aged 6 to 14.
ref: Lesson 12: Our Social and Economic Environment

evidence: Private schools must keep a quarter of the seats in the first class
add: Add that unrecognised schools cannot teach, with the fine up to Rs 1 lakh.
point: Private schools must reserve 25 per cent seats for poor children, cannot demand donation or interview children, and unrecognised schools cannot teach.
ref: Lesson 12: Our Social and Economic Environment

evidence: The money a government office spends came from the people
point: The Right to Information Act 2005 lets every citizen ask how public money and works are used, because public money comes from taxes everyone pays.
ref: Lesson 12: Our Social and Economic Environment

evidence: The fee is 10 rupees for central government offices
add: Add: apply on plain paper, give no reason; per-page copy and CD fees vary, so say Rs 2 a page.
point: To ask for information, apply on plain paper to the Public Information Officer with your details and a fee, giving no reason.
ref: Lesson 12: Our Social and Economic Environment

evidence: the answer must come within 48 hours
add: Add the penalty: Rs 250 a day, up to Rs 25,000, and the appeal route.
point: Officers must reply within 30 days (48 hours if life or liberty is at stake), and delay can bring a penalty on the officer.
ref: Lesson 12: Our Social and Economic Environment

evidence: Some things may be kept secret
add: Add the exemptions: threats to unity or security, court-banned material, parliamentary privilege, foreign confidences, risk to life.
point: Some information need not be given: anything that threatens national unity or security, court-banned material, parliamentary privilege, foreign confidences and risks to life.
ref: Lesson 12: Our Social and Economic Environment

evidence: It promised every village household up to 100 days of paid work a year
add: DATED: unit notes the 100 days were replaced by 125 days from 1 July 2026.
point: MNREGA 2005 guarantees 100 days of paid unskilled manual work per financial year to rural households, so people need not leave their villages for work.
ref: Lesson 12: Our Social and Economic Environment

evidence: They get a free job card. If no work is given within 15 days
add: Add that a third of workers must be women, and the job card's validity.
point: Rural adults apply to the Gram Panchayat for a free job card and work within 15 days; a third of workers must be women.
ref: Lesson 12: Our Social and Economic Environment

evidence: A work site must have drinking water, shade and first aid.
add: Add the crèche, equal wages for men and women, and injury and death payments.
point: MNREGA wages are paid within 15 days into bank or post accounts, equal for men and women, with free water, shade and crèche.
ref: Lesson 12: Our Social and Economic Environment

evidence: the police and the fire service do
point: Places like shops, roads, health centres, police stations and schools connect people, and each one does a service for the community.
ref: Unit 1 Our Community, Ch 1 Living Together

evidence: test whether agreeing a rule stops a shared pond running out
add: Add how to use, clean and decorate shared places like parks together for occasions.
point: Parks, roads and other public places are shared, so people must use, clean and decorate them together.
ref: Unit 1 Our Community, Ch 1 Living Together

point: Van Mahotsav is a tree-planting festival held in the rainy season, about 1 to 7 July, to make the earth greener.
ref: Unit 1 Our Community, Ch 1 Living Together

evidence: test whether agreeing a rule stops a shared pond running out
add: Add a group task where a family splits cleaning, planting, watering and cooking into named jobs.
point: Families and children share a community task by splitting it into jobs such as cleaning, planting, watering and cooking.
ref: Unit 1 Our Community, Ch 1 Living Together

evidence: A drawing or a few lines about the worker: their tool, their name
point: Local workers keep the neighbourhood going, and each has an occupation, a job and a tool.
ref: Unit 1 Our Community, Ch 1 Living Together

evidence: Meet a Helper: a short interview with a worker near home
point: Interviewing family or neighbours about their work reveals what they like, what tools they use and what challenges they face.
ref: Unit 1 Our Community, Ch 1 Living Together

point: After floods cut off schools and hospitals, a village built a bamboo and stone bridge in two days, showing a community responding together.
ref: Unit 1 Our Community, Ch 1 Living Together

evidence: Hives, mounds and nests: how bees, wasps and termites share the work
point: Ant colonies and bee hives work like communities, with each member doing a special job such as finding food or guarding the young.
ref: Unit 1 Our Community, Ch 1 Living Together

evidence: Peels and dry leaves left in a pot with air holes turn into compost in about two months
point: Leaves from a feast buried in a pit break down into manure, which improves the soil.
ref: Unit 1 Our Community, Ch 1 Living Together

add: NOT SCIENCE: Add Bhela Ghar in Assam and Khetala helpers in Sikkim as examples of working together at festivals.
point: Festivals and harvests show cooperation, such as the Bhela Ghar hut built during Magh Bihu in Assam and the Khetala helpers of Sikkim.
ref: Unit 1 Our Community, Ch 1 Living Together

evidence: they bring milk, sweep the road, teach, nurse and deliver letters
add: Add school staff (teacher, caretaker, bus driver) and how each role helps the school run.
point: Schools run on many roles, such as teachers, caretakers and bus drivers, and teamwork makes the school work.
ref: Unit 1 Our Community, Ch 1 Living Together

evidence: An auto-rickshaw is a three-wheeled vehicle.
add: Add metro trains and flyovers, and how a flyover lifts traffic above a busy crossing to save time.
point: Buses, e-rickshaws, metro trains and flyovers move people faster, and flyovers lift traffic above busy crossings to save time.
ref: Unit 1 Our Community, Ch 2 Exploring Our Neighbourhood

evidence: To reach further, they beat drums, lit fires and sent runners and pigeons
point: Communication has changed from drumbeats and carvings to messengers, post, phones, radio, television and the internet.
ref: Unit 1 Our Community, Ch 2 Exploring Our Neighbourhood

evidence: It tells the post office which area a letter must go to.
add: Add the letter's journey: postbox, postman, sorting by region, and money orders and parcels.
point: A post office sorts letters by region and sends them on, and it also offers services such as money orders and parcels.
ref: Unit 1 Our Community, Ch 2 Exploring Our Neighbourhood

evidence: people could travel across India in days instead of weeks
add: Add how slow letters were (weeks), and the risk of false news today; check whether news is true.
point: Comparing past and present communication shows that letters were slow, while messages are quick but can spread false news.
ref: Unit 1 Our Community, Ch 2 Exploring Our Neighbourhood

evidence: the doctor gives tablets to only one
add: Add hospital staff, doctors and nurses, and what each one does, including an eye check-up camp.
point: A hospital or health centre has staff, such as doctors and nurses, who treat patients and give medicines.
ref: Unit 1 Our Community, Ch 2 Exploring Our Neighbourhood

point: Banks keep money safe and help families save; an ATM gives cash at any time, and phones now send money online.
ref: Unit 1 Our Community, Ch 2 Exploring Our Neighbourhood

point: Money was invented to replace barter, the swapping of goods, because finding a trade partner and a fair exchange was hard.
ref: Unit 1 Our Community, Ch 2 Exploring Our Neighbourhood

evidence: the police and the fire service do
point: Public places such as libraries, post offices and police stations give services for health, safety, cleanliness and the environment.
ref: Unit 1 Our Community, Ch 2 Exploring Our Neighbourhood

add: NOT SCIENCE: Add a small monthly money plan (savings versus spending, with reasons) to the money-basics unit.
point: A child plans a small monthly sum by splitting it between savings and expenses, and gives a reason for each amount.
ref: Unit 1 Our Community, Ch 2 Exploring Our Neighbourhood

point: An Indian currency note shows its value, several languages, and pictures or symbols that can be read closely.
ref: Unit 1 Our Community, Ch 2 Exploring Our Neighbourhood

evidence: north, south, east and west work for anyone
point: On a map, north is up, south is down, east is right and west is left, and east can be found from the rising sun.
ref: Unit 1 Our Community, Ch 2 Exploring Our Neighbourhood

evidence: while left and right change when a person turns
point: Landmarks and words such as left, right, forward and backward let a child describe a route so a friend can find a place.
ref: Unit 1 Our Community, Ch 2 Exploring Our Neighbourhood

evidence: the police and the fire service do
add: Add COVID-era health and sanitation workers and the vehicles each public service uses (patrol jeep).
point: During COVID-19 doctors, nurses, garbage collectors and shopkeepers kept neighbourhoods safe, and each public service uses people and vehicles.
ref: Unit 1 Our Community, Ch 2 Exploring Our Neighbourhood

evidence: We should feed every animal we see in the city, because feeding is kind.
add: Add forest and zoo visit rules: no feeding or teasing animals, no polythene, do not damage plants.
point: Forest and zoo visits need safety rules, such as not feeding or teasing animals, not damaging plants, and not littering or bringing polythene.
ref: Unit 2 Life Around Us, Ch 3 Nature Trail

evidence: Beaks and feet for different foods
add: Add a sort of forest animals into land and sky groups, naming one visible feature each, e.g. elephant trunk.
point: Forest animals can be sorted into animals on land and birds in the sky, and each has a visible feature that helps it live.
ref: Unit 2 Life Around Us, Ch 3 Nature Trail

evidence: a squirrel on the wire
add: Add the Indian giant squirrel (large and red) and spectacled monkey, Tripura's state animal, to compare with local squirrels.
point: The Indian giant squirrel is large and red, and the spectacled monkey, Tripura's state animal, has white rings round its eyes.
ref: Unit 2 Life Around Us, Ch 3 Nature Trail

evidence: A tiger's pugmark in mud: four round toe marks
add: Add tracks in pond mud from gaur, deer and rabbit, guessing the animal, and drawing a footprint.
point: Footprints in pond mud show which animals came to drink, so a track can be used to guess who passed by.
ref: Unit 2 Life Around Us, Ch 3 Nature Trail

evidence: A sunbird has a long, thin, curved beak that reaches the nectar
point: A bird's beak and claws show what it eats: an eagle's curved beak catches prey and a sunbird's long beak reaches nectar.
ref: Unit 2 Life Around Us, Ch 3 Nature Trail

evidence: A call is a short sound a bird makes to send a message.
add: Add a bird diary: colours of head, back, wing and throat, beak, how it moves, and where it sits.
point: A bird diary records what a bird looks like, how it moves and eats, and where it sits, after first listening to birdsong.
ref: Unit 2 Life Around Us, Ch 3 Nature Trail

evidence: a frog on a leaf with a round eardrum
add: Add water animals: fish fins, gharial's narrow snout, turtle shell and webbed feet, frogs on land and in water.
point: Water animals have special features: fish have fins, gharial a narrow snout, turtles shells and webbed feet, and frogs live on land and in water.
ref: Unit 2 Life Around Us, Ch 3 Nature Trail

evidence: touch each arriving bee with their antennae
add: Name insect features: three pairs of legs, one pair of antennae, and wings on flies and grasshoppers.
point: Insects have three pairs of legs and one pair of antennae, and some, like flies and grasshoppers, also have two pairs of wings.
ref: Unit 2 Life Around Us, Ch 3 Nature Trail

evidence: A mango leaf, a tulsi leaf and a blade of grass are all leaves.
add: Add leaf observation: colour, shape, texture, smell, vein patterns, and a crayon rubbing of the outline.
point: Leaves differ in colour, shape, texture and smell, and their veins follow two arrangements; a crayon rubbing shows the leaf's outline.
ref: Unit 2 Life Around Us, Ch 3 Nature Trail

evidence: Six kinds of links in a web of life
point: In the Web of Life game, each living thing is linked to others, and removing one player weakens the whole web.
ref: Unit 2 Life Around Us, Ch 3 Nature Trail

evidence: Walk there with a local guide and ask about the rules of the forest.
add: Add a forest-scene role-play and a nature walk where children name local plants and animals and features.
point: Role-plays and forest scenes teach children to protect plants and animals, and a nature guide must know local species and their features.
ref: Unit 2 Life Around Us, Ch 3 Nature Trail

evidence: Madhav Gadgil and other ecologists
point: Plants and animals depend on each other, and a nature scientist studies these links, such as the state animal, bird and plant.
ref: Unit 2 Life Around Us, Ch 3 Nature Trail

add: Add Palash, the flame of the forest, and local flower names, with a name-and-draw task, to a plants-of-India unit.
point: The Palash tree is called the flame of the forest because its orange-red flowers colour the forest, and flowers have local names.
ref: Unit 2 Life Around Us, Ch 4 Growing up with Nature

evidence: all hold energy that came from sunlight, either lately or long ago
add: Add solar panels turning sunlight into electricity to run a fan and bulb in a village.
point: Solar panels turn sunlight into electricity, so a village can power fans and bulbs.
ref: Unit 2 Life Around Us, Ch 4 Growing up with Nature

evidence: Terracotta is baked clay, usually reddish brown
add: Add village walls of cow dung and hay, painted with natural rice-flour paint, and why they suit village life.
point: Traditional village houses are built from clay, hay, cow dung and other natural materials, and walls are painted with natural colour.
ref: Unit 2 Life Around Us, Ch 4 Growing up with Nature

evidence: A way of making a pattern by tying and dyeing the threads
add: Add a plant-dye procedure: boil beetroot, hibiscus or marigold, strain, and soak cloth overnight.
point: Natural dye is made by boiling plant parts in water, straining the liquid and soaking cloth in it overnight.
ref: Unit 2 Life Around Us, Ch 4 Growing up with Nature

evidence: a bunch of neem leaves and a tulsi pot on the windowsill
add: Add traditional grain storage: neem leaves in earthen pots and cow-dung-coated baskets, and why pests stay out.
point: Grain stored in earthen pots lined with neem leaves, and in bamboo baskets coated with cow dung, stays safe from insects and pests.
ref: Unit 2 Life Around Us, Ch 4 Growing up with Nature

evidence: a bunch of neem leaves and a tulsi pot on the windowsill
add: Add what a first-aid box holds and why first aid matters, linked to the medicines unit.
point: Neem oil repels mosquitoes, a first-aid box holds medicines, and plants such as tulsi and ajwain have medicinal uses.
ref: Unit 2 Life Around Us, Ch 4 Growing up with Nature

add: NOT SCIENCE: Add regional folk dances, dhol and nagada music, and prayers to nature, to a festivals unit.
point: Village festivals include prayers to nature, dhol and nagada music, traditional clothes and dances.
ref: Unit 2 Life Around Us, Ch 4 Growing up with Nature

evidence: Groves work as small nature reserves
point: Sacred groves are small forest patches protected by local communities, where trees and wildlife are kept safe and people gather to worship.
ref: Unit 2 Life Around Us, Ch 4 Growing up with Nature

add: NOT SCIENCE: Add festivals that honour trees and animals: Vat Purnima banyan, Kaziranga Elephant Festival, Jenu Kurubas bees.
point: Many festivals honour plants and animals, such as Vat Purnima for the banyan tree and the Kaziranga Elephant Festival; Jenu Kurubas sing to bees.
ref: Unit 2 Life Around Us, Ch 4 Growing up with Nature

evidence: how much can we take and still leave enough
point: People use nature for food, cotton, and neem medicine, but overusing these resources causes problems such as depleted forests and polluted water.
ref: Unit 2 Life Around Us, Ch 4 Growing up with Nature

evidence: The plastic is a strip of an empty milk packet
add: Add feeding birds with water and grain, planting trees and school clean-up drives as ways to protect nature.
point: Caring for nature means reducing paper waste, saying no to plastic, planting trees, feeding birds and holding clean-up drives.
ref: Unit 2 Life Around Us, Ch 4 Growing up with Nature

evidence: sort plants into trees, shrubs, herbs, climbers and creepers
add: Add planning a herbal garden: draw and name each herb, including less-liked ones, and the part used.
point: A herbal garden can be planned with favourite herbs, including ones the child likes less, each drawn and named.
ref: Unit 2 Life Around Us, Ch 4 Growing up with Nature

evidence: A Gujarati thali has roti, dal, rice, a vegetable
point: A school food festival brings regional dishes from many states, showing how food varies across the country.
ref: Unit 3 Health and Well-being, Ch 5 Food for Health

evidence: sweet jaggery, sour tamarind, salt, bitter neem flowers, hot pepper
point: The six tastes, shad rasa, are sweet, sour, salty, pungent, bitter and astringent, and a balanced meal blends them, as in Ugadi Pachadi.
ref: Unit 3 Health and Well-being, Ch 5 Food for Health

evidence: name some millets and why farmers grow them in dry land
point: Millets such as jowar, bajra, jau and ragi are rich in nutrients and were eaten in different seasons.
ref: Unit 3 Health and Well-being, Ch 5 Food for Health

evidence: Energy-giving, body-building and protective foods
point: Food gives energy, helps the body grow and protects it from disease, and no single food has all the nutrients the body needs.
ref: Unit 3 Health and Well-being, Ch 5 Food for Health

evidence: Many chips, instant noodles, fizzy drinks and packet biscuits are ultra-processed
point: Junk food such as chips, soft drinks, burgers and pizza is high in oil, salt or sugar, so it should be eaten rarely.
ref: Unit 3 Health and Well-being, Ch 5 Food for Health

evidence: I can make a balanced plate or thali from the food in my own kitchen
point: A week's food diary shows what is eaten, which items are healthy, and which food groups are missing from the daily plan.
ref: Unit 3 Health and Well-being, Ch 5 Food for Health

evidence: sweat, breath and urine as ways of removing waste
add: Add water's other jobs: helping digest food and keeping skin healthy, with daily drinking.
point: Water helps digest food, keeps the skin healthy, and removes waste through urine, sweat and faeces.
ref: Unit 3 Health and Well-being, Ch 5 Food for Health

evidence: what cooking does to food for ever
add: Name cooking methods (steam, boil, fry, roast, grill, bake) and no-cook foods such as salads.
point: Food is cooked by steaming, boiling, frying, roasting, grilling or baking, while some foods such as salads need no cooking.
ref: Unit 3 Health and Well-being, Ch 5 Food for Health

evidence: guess a food from its label
add: Add reading a packet's best-before date and its two main ingredients.
point: A packaged food label shows the expiry date and main ingredients, which help a buyer decide before eating.
ref: Unit 3 Health and Well-being, Ch 5 Food for Health

evidence: A Gujarati thali has bajra or wheat roti, dal, kadhi, a vegetable
add: Add a family task: who cooks at home, and listing the items of your own regional thali.
point: Every region has its own thali with many tastes, and families share the work of cooking, so everyone can learn.
ref: Unit 3 Health and Well-being, Ch 5 Food for Health

evidence: I can name protective foods and say what vitamins, minerals and fibre do
point: A food collage sorts pictures into energy, body-building and protective foods, and a word search finds food words.
ref: Unit 3 Health and Well-being, Ch 5 Food for Health

add: NOT SCIENCE: Add a short reflection on favourite foods, games and play that bring happiness.
point: People feel happy when they eat favourite foods or play games, and foods from grains, pulses and vegetables bring joy.
ref: Unit 3 Health and Well-being, Ch 6 Happy and Healthy Living

point: A rice or wheat grain travels from farm to plate through sowing, growing, harvesting, transport, selling and cooking, with many people involved.
ref: Unit 3 Health and Well-being, Ch 6 Happy and Healthy Living

evidence: how soil holds water for roots
point: Soil, water, sunlight, earthworms, cattle and farmers all help a grain grow, so a missing element breaks the journey.
ref: Unit 3 Health and Well-being, Ch 6 Happy and Healthy Living

evidence: Pongal in January is cooked from the new rice harvest
point: Festivals such as Makar Sankranti, Akshay Tritiya, Onam and Lohri show gratitude to Mother Nature for food.
ref: Unit 3 Health and Well-being, Ch 6 Happy and Healthy Living

evidence: I can explain what chewing and saliva do
point: Mindful eating means feeling, chewing slowly and noticing taste and texture; the tongue moves food and the teeth break it down.
ref: Unit 3 Health and Well-being, Ch 6 Happy and Healthy Living

point: Wasting food disrespects the work of everyone who grew it, and a week's food record helps a child notice and avoid waste.
ref: Unit 3 Health and Well-being, Ch 6 Happy and Healthy Living

evidence: I can do three yoga poses and slow breathing
add: Add running, cycling and skipping as daily activities, and how yoga improves posture.
point: Physical activities such as running, cycling and skipping keep the body strong, and yoga improves posture.
ref: Unit 3 Health and Well-being, Ch 6 Happy and Healthy Living

evidence: Exercise and rest: why muscles get tired, and what sleep does
point: Sleep takes away tiredness; without enough, people feel sleepy and irritable, so rest matters as much as food and exercise.
ref: Unit 3 Health and Well-being, Ch 6 Happy and Healthy Living

evidence: which touches are not OK, and who my trusted adults are
point: Safe touch comforts while unsafe touch makes a person uneasy, and a child can say no firmly and tell a trusted adult.
ref: Unit 3 Health and Well-being, Ch 6 Happy and Healthy Living

evidence: I can make a balanced plate or thali from the food in my own kitchen
add: Add a daily habit plan: waking early, less TV or mobile, and one habit the child will try.
point: A balanced plate for breakfast, lunch and dinner, and a daily habits plan such as waking early and less TV, support healthy living.
ref: Unit 3 Health and Well-being, Ch 6 Happy and Healthy Living

evidence: spin a coin on different floors
point: Some objects spin well, such as coins, bangles and tops, while erasers do not, and children observe and predict before spinning.
ref: Unit 4 Things Around Us, Ch 7 How Things Work

evidence: An off-centre pencil makes the top wobble and fall fast
point: A spinner with the toothpick at the centre stays upright and spins, while one with the toothpick off-centre does not spin well.
ref: Unit 4 Things Around Us, Ch 7 How Things Work

evidence: spin a colour wheel to turn colours back into white
add: Add a square card that looks round when spun, and painted spinners whose colours blend.
point: A square card looks circular when spun, and painted spinners show their colours blended; ceiling fans and potter's wheels also spin.
ref: Unit 4 Things Around Us, Ch 7 How Things Work

evidence: A steel ship floats, but a small pebble sinks
point: Paper boats float or flip, and testing leaves, nails, bowls and stones in water shows which things float and which sink.
ref: Unit 4 Things Around Us, Ch 7 How Things Work

evidence: The big rolling pin floated, and so did a tiny matchstick
point: Heavy objects can float and light ones can sink, so weight alone does not decide whether an object floats.
ref: Unit 4 Things Around Us, Ch 7 How Things Work

evidence: A ball of foil sinks, but the same foil folded into a boat floats
point: Reshaping aluminium foil changes floating: a spread or cup-shaped foil floats, while a tight ball sinks because it traps less air.
ref: Unit 4 Things Around Us, Ch 7 How Things Work

evidence: Engineers choose materials for joints too
point: Groups design boats from paper, cardboard, ice-cream sticks or shells, then compare strengths and challenges and improve them.
ref: Unit 4 Things Around Us, Ch 7 How Things Work

evidence: A ball of foil sinks, but the same foil folded into a boat floats
add: Add balancing a tilting figure by moving its weight or position, not only changing a sinking object's shape.
point: A tilting figure can be balanced by changing its weight or position, and a sinking object can be made to float by changing its shape.
ref: Unit 4 Things Around Us, Ch 7 How Things Work

evidence: A steel ship floats, but a small pebble sinks
point: Everyday objects such as wax, cork, thermocol, marble, potato and lemon can be sorted into things that float and things that sink.
ref: Unit 4 Things Around Us, Ch 7 How Things Work

evidence: Two ideas, one question: how to tell explanations apart
add: Add a spinner-slowing question prompt and the charkha twisting cotton into thread.
point: Curiosity drives questions, such as why a spinner slows and shakes, and how a charkha twists cotton into thread.
ref: Unit 4 Things Around Us, Ch 7 How Things Work

point: Paper comes from trees, so books, newspapers, napkins and chart paper all come from trees, and recycling saves them.
ref: Unit 4 Things Around Us, Ch 8 How Things are Made

point: Recycled paper is made by soaking torn newspaper with fenugreek seeds as a binder, blending, rolling it thin and drying it.
ref: Unit 4 Things Around Us, Ch 8 How Things are Made

add: Add a paper-colouring test with turmeric, spinach, beetroot and henna, keeping the amount of each the same.
point: Paper can be coloured with natural ingredients such as turmeric, spinach, beetroot and henna, and the same amount of each keeps the test fair.
ref: Unit 4 Things Around Us, Ch 8 How Things are Made

point: Making paper from wood pulp needs many trees, water and energy, so paper should be used only when needed.
ref: Unit 4 Things Around Us, Ch 8 How Things are Made

add: Add earlier writing materials (cloth, leaves, palm-leaf talapatra) and banana-fibre paper as an eco option.
point: Earlier people wrote on cloth, leaves and wooden boards and palm leaves called talapatra, and banana fibre can make eco-friendly paper.
ref: Unit 4 Things Around Us, Ch 8 How Things are Made

evidence: Choosing materials: no material is best, so how do we choose?
add: Add paper types matched to jobs: tissue absorbs water, thick cardboard for boxes, Braille paper for raised dots.
point: Different papers suit different jobs: tissue absorbs water, cardboard is thick for boxes, and Braille paper carries raised dots for reading.
ref: Unit 4 Things Around Us, Ch 8 How Things are Made

point: The 5Rs of waste management are Refuse, Reduce, Reuse, Repurpose and Recycle, each a step to cut down waste.
ref: Unit 4 Things Around Us, Ch 8 How Things are Made

point: Everyday actions, such as using cloth bags, painting old bottles or making paper envelopes, each belong to one of the 5Rs.
ref: Unit 4 Things Around Us, Ch 8 How Things are Made

point: Used paper can be turned into toys, decorations, greeting cards and masks, which shows creative reuse.
ref: Unit 4 Things Around Us, Ch 8 How Things are Made

point: A 5R plan for paper at home and school, with one step for each R, reduces paper waste.
ref: Unit 4 Things Around Us, Ch 8 How Things are Made

point: A paper mill field trip shows how paper is made at scale, and the Braille system lets visually challenged people read by touch.
ref: Unit 4 Things Around Us, Ch 8 How Things are Made

point: Four landforms, plains, deserts, coastal regions and mountains, shape the food, clothing, houses, festivals and art of the people who live there.
ref: Unit 5 Our Environment, Ch 9 Different Lands, Different Lives

point: The Amritsar plains have rich, fertile soil for farming, and people eat makki di roti and sarson da saag with lassi.
ref: Unit 5 Our Environment, Ch 9 Different Lands, Different Lives

evidence: The khejri tree sends her roots many metres down.
point: Deserts are dry with little rain; cactus, khejri and babool survive on little water, and camels suit the sandy land.
ref: Unit 5 Our Environment, Ch 9 Different Lands, Different Lives

add: Add coastal fishing communities, sea creatures and Puri's coast to the coast-versus-desert comparison.
point: Coastal regions have fishing, sea shells, sand art and sea creatures, and Puri in Odisha shows these features.
ref: Unit 5 Our Environment, Ch 9 Different Lands, Different Lives

point: Strong winds and cyclones hit coastal areas and harm people, animals and trees, but early warnings and preparation save lives.
ref: Unit 5 Our Environment, Ch 9 Different Lands, Different Lives

add: Add cold, steep, snow-capped Himalayan mountains and how that climate shapes houses, clothes and trees.
point: Mountains are rocky, cold and steep, often snow-capped in the Himalayas, and their climate shapes houses, clothes and trees.
ref: Unit 5 Our Environment, Ch 9 Different Lands, Different Lives

point: Landslides in the mountains during rain are dangerous, and communities help people who lose homes or are hurt in disasters.
ref: Unit 5 Our Environment, Ch 9 Different Lands, Different Lives

add: NOT SCIENCE: add landform-linked traditions (Loosong, Namsoong, khartal, bandhini) to a society unit.
point: Traditions are tied to landforms, such as Loosong and Namsoong in Sikkim, Rajasthan dance and folk music, and clothes suited to each region.
ref: Unit 5 Our Environment, Ch 9 Different Lands, Different Lives

point: A comparison table of plains, deserts, coasts and mountains covers trees, animals, housing, clothing, food, festivals and art.
ref: Unit 5 Our Environment, Ch 9 Different Lands, Different Lives

add: Plan covers landforms; add the design-your-landform task with benefits and difficulties.
point: A child designs a landform by combining features from mountains, plains, coasts and deserts, then explains its benefits and difficulties.
ref: Unit 5 Our Environment, Ch 9 Different Lands, Different Lives

add: Add a survey of friends' holiday regions and a compare-with-own-place activity.
point: A survey of friends' holiday places records the region type and special feature of each, then compares them with one's own.
ref: Unit 5 Our Environment, Ch 9 Different Lands, Different Lives

add: Add observing sky colour, Sun and Moon through morning, afternoon and night, with a table.
point: The sky changes through the day: its colour, the Sun, the Moon's size and shape, and the activities of living things all vary.
ref: Unit 5 Our Environment, Ch 10 Our Sky

evidence: the Sun is a star, a huge ball of very hot gas
point: The Sun is the brightest object in the sky, and its light hides the stars in daytime; it gives us light and heat.
ref: Unit 5 Our Environment, Ch 10 Our Sky

evidence: rising in the east and setting in the west
point: The Sun appears to rise in the east, climb overhead and then move down toward the west, and living things change at sunrise and sunset.
ref: Unit 5 Our Environment, Ch 10 Our Sky

point: Shadows are long in the morning, short at noon and long in the evening, and they point in opposite directions in the morning and evening.
ref: Unit 5 Our Environment, Ch 10 Our Sky

evidence: The huge sundial at Jantar Mantar in Jaipur casts a shadow
point: Shadows change as the Sun moves, and a sundial uses shadows to tell time, as the Samrat Yantra at Jantar Mantar does.
ref: Unit 5 Our Environment, Ch 10 Our Sky

evidence: make a shadow puppet
point: Shadow puppetry uses cut-out shapes held against light, a practice in India for a long time.
ref: Unit 5 Our Environment, Ch 10 Our Sky

evidence: constellation pictures
point: After sunset thousands of stars appear in patterns, and children draw the patterns they see and compare them with others.
ref: Unit 5 Our Environment, Ch 10 Our Sky

evidence: how to predict any phase
point: The Moon's shape changes night to night, from full to C-shaped to half, and is unseen at new Moon; this cycle guided early calendars.
ref: Unit 5 Our Environment, Ch 10 Our Sky

evidence: Hindu festival dates are set by the tithi, which tracks the Moon's age.
point: Festivals follow the Moon: Diwali on a moonless night, Raksha Bandhan and Buddha Purnima on a full Moon, Eid after new Moon's first sighting.
ref: Unit 5 Our Environment, Ch 10 Our Sky

evidence: India's Chandrayaan-3
add: Add the Vikram lander touching down on the Moon on 23 August 2023 and collecting surface data.
point: India's Vikram lander touched down on the Moon on 23 August 2023 and collected data on its surface, part of Chandrayaan.
ref: Unit 5 Our Environment, Ch 10 Our Sky

evidence: the day from one noon to the next is 24 hours
point: Children compare day and night, ask questions about the Sun's movement, and reason why shadows change at different times.
ref: Unit 5 Our Environment, Ch 10 Our Sky

evidence: Fresh water and salt water: why so little of Earth's water can be drunk
point: Most water on Earth is salty, so freshwater is scarce, yet every living being depends on it.
ref: Unit 1, Chapter 1: Water — The Essence of Life

evidence: why every substance has its own melting point
point: Water exists as liquid, ice and vapour, and each form can change into the others and back again.
ref: Unit 1, Chapter 1: Water — The Essence of Life

evidence: the water cycle explained with particles
point: Heat turns water into vapour, which forms clouds that fall as rain, snow or hail, completing the water cycle.
ref: Unit 1, Chapter 1: Water — The Essence of Life

evidence: little water can soak in
point: Rainwater soaks through soil as groundwater, which we reach with wells and handpumps, but cemented surfaces stop this recharge.
ref: Unit 1, Chapter 1: Water — The Essence of Life

point: Rivers start in hills and follow the slope of the land, and flowing water can change the shape of land over time.
ref: Unit 1, Chapter 1: Water — The Essence of Life

evidence: a purple swamphen walking on floating leaves
add: Add pond plant types (rooted lotus, floating-leaved water lily, free-floating water hyacinth) and fish fins.
point: Animals and plants in freshwater have features such as fins, rooted or floating leaves, and long legs that suit life in water.
ref: Unit 1, Chapter 1: Water — The Essence of Life

evidence: A waxy band around the xylem
add: Add the waxy leaf coating that cuts water loss, and the wax-drop test.
point: A waxy coating on leaves makes them waterproof and keeps too much water from getting inside the plant.
ref: Unit 1, Chapter 1: Water — The Essence of Life

evidence: what happens when one link disappears
point: In a river food chain each living being depends on others, so losing one kind of animal affects all the rest.
ref: Unit 1, Chapter 1: Water — The Essence of Life

add: Dams are in the rivers plan (sci.water.rivers.L5); harvesting and tanks are here.
point: Water is limited and shared, so cities plan storage, recharge and careful use, through dams, watersheds and village-level harvesting.
ref: Unit 1, Chapter 1: Water — The Essence of Life

add: Add a pond-creature observation: mouth position, movement and body parts matched to its way of life.
point: Visiting a pond and recording what creatures and plants look like, and how they move and feed, links body parts to way of life.
ref: Unit 1, Chapter 1: Water — The Essence of Life

point: The Godavari starts in the Western Ghats, flows about 1,465 km and reaches the Bay of Bengal, making it India's second longest river.
ref: Unit 1, Chapter 2: Journey of a River

add: Add perennial and seasonal rivers, which the plan does not yet name.
point: Rivers that flow all year are perennial, while seasonal rivers flow only after rain, and tributaries feed bigger rivers.
ref: Unit 1, Chapter 2: Journey of a River

evidence: where mangrove trees take root
point: Where a river meets the sea it spreads into a delta, and mangrove forests grow where fresh water and salt water mix.
ref: Unit 1, Chapter 2: Journey of a River

point: People depend on the river for drinking, cooking, farming, factories and jobs, which is why towns grew up beside it.
ref: Unit 1, Chapter 2: Journey of a River

point: Dams store water for drinking, farming and electricity, but they flood land and force people and animals to move away.
ref: Unit 1, Chapter 2: Journey of a River

evidence: uses up the oxygen that fish breathe
point: Waste, plastic and dirty water from homes and factories pollute rivers, harming fish, birds and the people who drink the water.
ref: Unit 1, Chapter 2: Journey of a River

evidence: Dissolving: what water takes, what oil takes
point: Some substances dissolve in water, like sugar, while oil does not, and dissolved chemicals can hide in water that looks clean.
ref: Unit 1, Chapter 2: Journey of a River

evidence: The nitrogen in fertiliser feeds crops, and also feeds algae in a pond.
point: Fertiliser washed into rivers feeds plants and algae until they cover the surface, choking fish and making the water unsafe to drink.
ref: Unit 1, Chapter 2: Journey of a River

add: Add trees and soil slowing runoff, which the plan does not yet name.
point: Heavy rain makes a river overflow and flood homes, fields and roads, and trees slow runoff and help soil soak up water.
ref: Unit 1, Chapter 2: Journey of a River

point: Flood safety means preparing before, staying safe during and cleaning up after, and communities plan for elders, people with disability and animals.
ref: Unit 1, Chapter 2: Journey of a River

evidence: This card is about water shortages
add: Add three everyday water-saving habits and an excess example (Bengaluru floods).
point: A river that runs dry or floods shows that both shortage and excess of water harm people, so water must be used wisely.
ref: Unit 1, Chapter 2: Journey of a River

evidence: hilsa swim up the rivers to lay their eggs
point: Rivers support many living things: hilsa fish migrate from the sea to lay eggs, and the Ganges river dolphin finds its way by sound.
ref: Unit 1, Chapter 2: Journey of a River

evidence: a living being too small to see without a microscope
point: Microbes are tiny living things found in soil, water, air, plants, animals and our bodies, and we need a microscope to see them.
ref: Unit 2, Chapter 3: The Mystery of Food

evidence: Honey keeps for years on a shelf, but cooked dal spoils in a day.
point: Microbes need moisture, air and a suitable temperature to grow, so removing any one of these can stop food from spoiling.
ref: Unit 2, Chapter 3: The Mystery of Food

evidence: Families dry food in the hot, dry months for this reason.
point: Sun-drying removes moisture from food like chillies, mango and tomato, so microbes cannot grow and the food lasts longer.
ref: Unit 2, Chapter 3: The Mystery of Food

evidence: a jar of mango pickle under oil
add: Add why oil keeps air and microbes away from pickle, and what happens without it.
point: Oil keeps air away from pickles, which stops microbes from growing and keeps the pickle safe to eat for a long time.
ref: Unit 2, Chapter 3: The Mystery of Food

evidence: Butter is about one-sixth water.
point: Cold temperature slows microbes, so fridges keep food longer, and clay matkas cool water without any electricity.
ref: Unit 2, Chapter 3: The Mystery of Food

evidence: Why food spoils, and how drying, salt, sugar and cold keep it
point: Traditional methods such as salt, sugar and spices also keep food from spoiling, and families still use them today.
ref: Unit 2, Chapter 3: The Mystery of Food

evidence: Idli batter, curd and bread: how tiny living beings make our food
point: Some microbes help make food: they make idli batter rise, turn milk into curd, and support digestion.
ref: Unit 2, Chapter 3: The Mystery of Food

add: Add indigestion causes (spoiled food, eating habits), curd as a remedy, and when to see a doctor.
point: Indigestion can come from spoiled food or bad eating habits, and curd can help, but severe cases need a doctor.
ref: Unit 2, Chapter 3: The Mystery of Food

add: Add seasonal and local produce freshness (lychee, local mango) to a food unit such as sci.food.balanced-diet.L5.
point: Fruits taste best in their season, and local produce is often fresher because it travels a shorter distance to reach us.
ref: Unit 2, Chapter 3: The Mystery of Food

evidence: teeth, saliva, stomach, intestines
point: Each kind of tooth has a job: incisors cut, canines tear, premolars crush and molars grind, and chewing starts digestion.
ref: Unit 2, Chapter 3: The Mystery of Food

evidence: A cavity hurts when it reaches the dentine
add: Add brushing and rinsing habits, eating fewer sweets, and when a dentist is needed.
point: Good oral hygiene means brushing, rinsing after meals and eating fewer sweets, and a dentist treats cavities.
ref: Unit 2, Chapter 3: The Mystery of Food

evidence: A dry mouth makes dry food very hard to swallow.
add: Add choking prevention: small mouthfuls, and no talking with food in the mouth.
point: Eating slowly in small mouthfuls, and not talking or laughing with food in the mouth, prevents choking.
ref: Unit 2, Chapter 3: The Mystery of Food

point: A green school is clean, safe and caring, where waste is managed, water and electricity are saved, and trees are planted and tended.
ref: Unit 2, Chapter 4: Our School — A Happy Place

evidence: how to map a place you cannot see
point: Walking around the school and drawing its map shows the main buildings, gate, paths and garden in their places.
ref: Unit 2, Chapter 4: Our School — A Happy Place

add: Add the explorer-team observation of electricity, water, greenery, waste and traffic.
point: Student explorer teams observe electricity, water, greenery, waste and traffic, then discuss what they found with the class.
ref: Unit 2, Chapter 4: Our School — A Happy Place

evidence: sort waste into organic and inorganic
point: Waste is best reduced by using less and reusing, then separated into wet and dry, with recyclers taking paper and other items.
ref: Unit 2, Chapter 4: Our School — A Happy Place

evidence: why a white roof keeps a house cooler
point: Shade, breezy windows and white roofs keep rooms cool, because white surfaces reflect sunlight while black surfaces absorb heat.
ref: Unit 2, Chapter 4: Our School — A Happy Place

point: A dripping tap can waste a surprising amount of water in a day, which a simple drip-timing measurement reveals.
ref: Unit 2, Chapter 4: Our School — A Happy Place

add: Add tree shade and temperature readings, and trees as homes for birds and insects, to an ecology unit.
point: Trees are homes for living things, clean the air, give shade and food to birds and insects, and keep the area cooler.
ref: Unit 2, Chapter 4: Our School — A Happy Place

add: NOT SCIENCE: traffic rules and a school-gate signboard.
point: Traffic rules keep roads safe, and a clear school-gate sign can warn drivers, parents and students to take care.
ref: Unit 2, Chapter 4: Our School — A Happy Place

evidence: What fire needs; fire safety
add: Add fire-drill steps: nearest exit, crawl low through smoke, never hide, go to the assembly point.
point: In a fire, move calmly to the nearest exit, crawl low through smoke, never hide, and gather at the assembly point.
ref: Unit 2, Chapter 4: Our School — A Happy Place

evidence: Waiting for your turn, putting a book back
point: Respect shows in everyday behaviour, such as waiting for turns, not bullying, not littering and not disturbing others.
ref: Unit 2, Chapter 4: Our School — A Happy Place

evidence: I can describe a day from another person's point of view
point: Children can raise awareness of community problems like road accidents and imagine the day of someone with different needs.
ref: Unit 2, Chapter 4: Our School — A Happy Place

evidence: Saffron stands for courage and giving things up for others.
point: The flag's saffron, white, green and blue Chakra each stand for a value: courage, peace, growth and duty.
ref: Unit 3, Chapter 5: Our Vibrant Country

add: NOT SCIENCE: the Constitution as the country's rulebook and why a country needs one.
point: Independence came on 15 August 1947, and Republic Day on 26 January 1950 marks the Constitution, the country's rulebook.
ref: Unit 3, Chapter 5: Our Vibrant Country

add: NOT SCIENCE: rupee-note symbols (monuments, spectacles, languages, Clean India mission).
point: A currency note carries many details, including languages, monuments, animals and spectacles that stand for the Clean India mission.
ref: Unit 3, Chapter 5: Our Vibrant Country

evidence: I can name India's national emblem, animal, bird and flower
point: The National Emblem's three lions, the national animal and the national bird are symbols that remind us who we are.
ref: Unit 3, Chapter 5: Our Vibrant Country

add: NOT SCIENCE: a common word (such as mango) across Indian languages.
point: India has over a thousand languages, and the same word, such as mango, is said differently in each one.
ref: Unit 3, Chapter 5: Our Vibrant Country

add: NOT SCIENCE: regional headgear and why helmets protect people.
point: Headgear such as the saafa or topi shows a person's region, beliefs or work, and helmets protect people on the job and on roads.
ref: Unit 3, Chapter 5: Our Vibrant Country

add: NOT SCIENCE: regional drums and dance forms by state.
point: Music and drums differ by region, shaped by local culture and materials, and each dance form has its own state of origin.
ref: Unit 3, Chapter 5: Our Vibrant Country

evidence: Partners and rivals: why very different living beings
point: A forest is stronger because its many species support each other, and a diverse country is stronger for the same reason.
ref: Unit 3, Chapter 5: Our Vibrant Country

evidence: India has people of many languages, foods, festivals and faiths
point: India's unity lies in its many languages, religions and traditions, woven together, while modern changes add new colours.
ref: Unit 3, Chapter 5: Our Vibrant Country

add: Add Indira Point's location in the Andaman and Nicobar Islands.
point: India's southernmost point, Indira Point, lies in the Andaman and Nicobar Islands, a chain of islands surrounded by water.
ref: Unit 3, Chapter 6: Some Unique Places

evidence: endemic and invasive species in India
point: The Andaman forests hold species found nowhere else, like the Andaman wood pigeon and hornbill, so these places need protection.
ref: Unit 3, Chapter 6: Some Unique Places

point: A paper tube stands upright once a base is added, just as tree roots hold a tree up, showing how nature inspires good design.
ref: Unit 3, Chapter 6: Some Unique Places

evidence: A reef coral. This animal has tiny algae living inside her body
add: Add coral reefs as shelter for fish, and why sea life matters to the whole Earth.
point: Corals are tiny living animals that build reefs giving shelter to fish and sea creatures, so sea life matters to the whole Earth.
ref: Unit 3, Chapter 6: Some Unique Places

evidence: whether mangroves protect villages from a tsunami
add: Add animals' and people's natural warning signs before the 2004 tsunami, with the North Sentinel Island example.
point: The people of North Sentinel Island keep their distance, and their reading of nature's signs may have helped them survive the 2004 tsunami.
ref: Unit 3, Chapter 6: Some Unique Places

evidence: where mangrove trees take root
add: Add mangrove roots that hold soil and block waves, with the Sundarbans example.
point: The Sundarbans is the largest mangrove forest, where the Ganga meets the sea, and mangrove roots hold soil and block waves.
ref: Unit 3, Chapter 6: Some Unique Places

evidence: I can explain four kinds of camouflage
point: Animals have special features to survive, such as markings that may confuse predators, and birds build nests that keep eggs safe.
ref: Unit 3, Chapter 6: Some Unique Places

add: NOT SCIENCE: the eight Northeast states and their crafts, houses and festivals.
point: The Northeast is the seven sister states plus Sikkim, a land of hills and forests where crafts, festivals and houses are shaped by nature.
ref: Unit 3, Chapter 6: Some Unique Places

evidence: people who protect forests
point: Communities protect nature with care: women teach children to guard the Hargila stork, and living root bridges are looked after.
ref: Unit 3, Chapter 6: Some Unique Places

evidence: The wet forest of the Western Ghats
add: Add the six states the Western Ghats cross and the rivers that begin there.
point: The Western Ghats are a long forested hill range crossing six states, home to lion-tailed macaques and the source of several rivers.
ref: Unit 3, Chapter 6: Some Unique Places

evidence: the size and shape of a protected area matter
point: Protected areas such as sanctuaries, national parks and tiger reserves keep forests and animals safe, and people saved Silent Valley from a dam.
ref: Unit 3, Chapter 6: Some Unique Places

evidence: the octopus with three hearts and clever arms
point: Sea animals have unusual features: starfish regrow arms, octopuses change colour, seahorses swim upright and turtles return to their birth beach.
ref: Unit 3, Chapter 6: Some Unique Places

evidence: how energy makes things happen
point: Energy is what makes things move, light up, make sound, do work and change temperature, and we use it every day.
ref: Unit 4, Chapter 7: Energy — How Things Work

evidence: A blown-up balloon stores it in the stretched rubber
add: Add moving air carrying energy, with the balloon rocket test.
point: Air rushing out of a balloon pushes it forward, showing that moving air carries energy that can move a balloon rocket along a string.
ref: Unit 4, Chapter 7: Energy — How Things Work

evidence: Vibration: how strings, skins and air columns make sound
point: Plucked rubber bands vibrate to make sound energy, and sunlight warms water, showing that the Sun gives heat energy.
ref: Unit 4, Chapter 7: Energy — How Things Work

evidence: Flowing and falling water turns
point: Sunlight, wind and flowing water can do work directly, such as drying clothes, turning a pinwheel and turning a water wheel.
ref: Unit 4, Chapter 7: Energy — How Things Work

evidence: breaks some of it down for energy
point: Living things get energy from food to move and stay active, and our bodies store extra energy for later use.
ref: Unit 4, Chapter 7: Energy — How Things Work

evidence: Cooking gas, petrol, diesel, coal, firewood and the oil in a diya are fuels.
point: Fuels such as petrol, diesel, cooking gas, wood and coal supply energy, and the oil in a diya acts as fuel.
ref: Unit 4, Chapter 7: Energy — How Things Work

evidence: A television with three small arrows coming out, labelled light, sound and heat.
point: Electric devices produce movement, sound, light, heat or cooling, and electricity also runs the machines that make many goods.
ref: Unit 4, Chapter 7: Energy — How Things Work

evidence: A 9 watt LED bulb gives about the same light as an old 60 watt
point: Energy efficiency means doing the same work with less energy, so LED bulbs give the same light while using less electricity.
ref: Unit 4, Chapter 7: Energy — How Things Work

evidence: Keeping safe with electricity: sockets, wires and water
point: Electricity can injure, so never touch wires or plugged-in parts, never poke sockets, stay away from boxes, and tell an adult about faults.
ref: Unit 4, Chapter 7: Energy — How Things Work

point: Burning coal makes smoke and harmful gases, while sun, wind and flowing water produce clean energy that does not pollute.
ref: Unit 4, Chapter 7: Energy — How Things Work

evidence: how it passes from thing to thing
point: Energy moves from a source to a type to a use, such as Sun, heat, drying clothes, and children trace these chains in a game.
ref: Unit 4, Chapter 7: Energy — How Things Work

evidence: a small flour mill called a gharat
add: Add cattle warming upper floors, Vaastu courtyards and wind-powered ships.
point: Traditional knowledge uses natural energy well: cattle warm the rooms above them, Vaastu plans homes around sunlight, and old ships sailed on wind.
ref: Unit 4, Chapter 7: Energy — How Things Work

evidence: This is weaving.
point: Weaving crosses one set of threads over and under another to make mats, baskets and cloth, and birds like the baya weaver do it too.
ref: Unit 4, Chapter 8: Clothes — How Things are Made

evidence: A frame or machine that holds the warp threads tight
point: Looked at closely, cloth shows a criss-cross pattern, and it is made by hand on a loom or by machines in textile mills.
ref: Unit 4, Chapter 8: Clothes — How Things are Made

evidence: Spinning
point: Spinning twists cotton fibres into thread, as a charkha does, and a single hair-like strand is called a fibre.
ref: Unit 4, Chapter 8: Clothes — How Things are Made

evidence: sort fibres into plant, animal and synthetic
point: Natural fibres such as cotton, wool, silk, linen, jute and bamboo come from plants and animals, and silk comes from silkworm cocoons.
ref: Unit 4, Chapter 8: Clothes — How Things are Made

evidence: sports jerseys are made of polyester or nylon
point: Synthetic fibres such as nylon, polyester, rayon and terylene are made from artificial materials, and most clothes mix natural and synthetic fibres.
ref: Unit 4, Chapter 8: Clothes — How Things are Made

evidence: A handloom is worked by a person's hands and feet
point: Handloom traditions such as Kanjeevaram, Pashmina, Ikat and Patola show great skill, and handloom weaving supports many families.
ref: Unit 4, Chapter 8: Clothes — How Things are Made

evidence: Cloth that is spun by hand and woven by hand.
point: Khadi, made by spinning and weaving one's own cloth, became a symbol of self-reliance and the freedom struggle that Gandhi ji promoted.
ref: Unit 4, Chapter 8: Clothes — How Things are Made

evidence: By the end I can sew a running stitch
add: Add what a broken thread does to a running stitch: the rest loosen.
point: A running stitch joins cloth with the needle going up and down in a line, and one broken thread can loosen the rest.
ref: Unit 4, Chapter 8: Clothes — How Things are Made

evidence: Kantha quilts are covered with rows of running stitch
point: Leaves and toothpicks can make plates and spoons, and old clothes can be reused or patched into quilts, which reduces waste.
ref: Unit 4, Chapter 8: Clothes — How Things are Made

evidence: Kantha quilts are covered with rows of running stitch
point: Embroideries such as Chikankari, Kantha, Phulkari and Khneng carry the stories of their places, people and traditions in each stitch.
ref: Unit 4, Chapter 8: Clothes — How Things are Made

evidence: cooking changes food for ever
add: Add sorting changes by speed: growing over years, yearly leaf-fall, and changes in minutes.
point: Looking back at changes in yourself, your school and your surroundings since Grade 3 shows that change is constant, some slow and some quick.
ref: Unit 5, Chapter 9: Rhythms of Nature

add: Add sorting changes by time scale: years, yearly cycles and minutes.
point: Some changes take years, some repeat yearly, and others take only minutes, such as the sky's colours or the Sun appearing to rise and set.
ref: Unit 5, Chapter 9: Rhythms of Nature

evidence: because the Earth turns
point: Day and night happen because Earth turns while the Sun stays in one place, so the Sun only seems to rise and set.
ref: Unit 5, Chapter 9: Rhythms of Nature

evidence: Guwahati
add: Add the share of Earth that is sea (about three-quarters) and a country in night when India has day.
point: A globe models Earth: seas cover about three-quarters of it, and when India has day, countries on the other side have night.
ref: Unit 5, Chapter 9: Rhythms of Nature

evidence: six ritus of about two months each
point: The same pattern of change repeats every year as seasons, and India has six seasons whose timing differs from region to region.
ref: Unit 5, Chapter 9: Rhythms of Nature

add: Add a seasons journal: four entries a year across five themes (plants, animals, weather, water, people).
point: A seasons' journal records one place four times a year across five themes, using simple notes, drawings or pasted finds.
ref: Unit 5, Chapter 9: Rhythms of Nature

add: Add a class observation wall chart and a pattern-finding activity to a seasons unit.
point: A class chart brings everyone's observations together by time period, so groups can spot patterns and tell a story about each period.
ref: Unit 5, Chapter 9: Rhythms of Nature

add: Add natural rain signs (koel calls, ants carrying eggs) and farmers' readings to sci.day-night-seasons.rhythms-of-nature.L5.
point: Nature gives seasonal signs, such as koels singing and ants carrying eggs to higher ground before rain, which farmers and villagers read.
ref: Unit 5, Chapter 9: Rhythms of Nature

point: Farmers grow different crops in different seasons, and many festivals, such as harvest festivals, are tied to the season.
ref: Unit 5, Chapter 9: Rhythms of Nature

add: Add regional names for the seasons and what people eat and wear in each.
point: Each region has its own names for the seasons, and food, clothes, festivals and nature all change with each one.
ref: Unit 5, Chapter 9: Rhythms of Nature

add: Add the view from space: one blue planet with no borders, and Rakesh Sharma's words.
point: Seen from space, Earth looks like one blue planet with no visible borders, though cities and villages are too small to see.
ref: Unit 5, Chapter 10: Earth — Our Shared Home

evidence: A bird's-eye view of a small neighbourhood
add: Add the address layers from house to planet, and locating India on a globe.
point: A full address moves outward from house to village, district, state, country and planet, and every place can be found on a globe.
ref: Unit 5, Chapter 10: Earth — Our Shared Home

evidence: How seeds travel: wings and wind, water, animals and people
add: Add how wind, water and animals carry things across lands, with two examples of 'no boundaries'.
point: Air, water, clouds, seeds and animals move freely across the world, so nature has no boundaries and everything is connected.
ref: Unit 5, Chapter 10: Earth — Our Shared Home

evidence: The rosy starling arrives in India around August or September
add: Add the route from Russia and Mongolia on a globe, and rosy starlings eating locusts that harm crops.
point: Rosy starlings fly thousands of kilometres each winter from Russia and Mongolia to India, where they eat locusts that harm crops.
ref: Unit 5, Chapter 10: Earth — Our Shared Home

add: NOT SCIENCE: Indian cattle breeds (Gir, Kankrej, Ongole) and Brazil's milk trade; add to an animals-and-people unit.
point: Indian cows taken to Brazil by Portuguese traders became so important that three Indian breeds now supply most of Brazil's milk.
ref: Unit 5, Chapter 10: Earth — Our Shared Home

add: NOT SCIENCE: yoga's origin in India and the 21 June International Day; add to a culture or health unit.
point: Yoga began in India over 3,000 years ago, spread through travellers and teachers, and the UN marks 21 June as International Day of Yoga.
ref: Unit 5, Chapter 10: Earth — Our Shared Home

add: NOT SCIENCE: chilli's route from South America to India, and similar food journeys; add to a food-history unit.
point: Chillies came from South America through Portuguese travellers 400 to 500 years ago, and now Indian food cannot be imagined without them.
ref: Unit 5, Chapter 10: Earth — Our Shared Home

add: NOT SCIENCE: goods traded in and out of India (jaggery, sugar, paper, dates); add to a trade and culture unit.
point: Goods and ideas moved both ways: jaggery and sugar went out from India, while paper, dates and lemons came in through trade.
ref: Unit 5, Chapter 10: Earth — Our Shared Home

add: NOT SCIENCE: marigold's journey from Mexico into Indian festivals; add to a festivals unit.
point: The marigold came from Mexico and now marks Indian festivals, showing how cultures adopt flowers and share their celebrations.
ref: Unit 5, Chapter 10: Earth — Our Shared Home

evidence: We have only one planet with life to study
add: Add Vasudhaiva Kutumbakam and why caring for our one living planet matters.
point: Vasudhaiva Kutumbakam means the world is one family, asking us to care for people, animals and the Earth, our only known home with life.
ref: Unit 5, Chapter 10: Earth — Our Shared Home

add: NOT SCIENCE: Ayurveda, chess and snakes and ladders spreading from India; add to a culture unit.
point: Ideas and games also travel: Ayurveda, chess and snakes and ladders all have roots in India and have spread to many lands.
ref: Unit 5, Chapter 10: Earth — Our Shared Home

add: NOT SCIENCE: define culture as an inherited way of life (customs, festivals, art, religion); add to a culture unit.
point: Culture is a way of life inherited from forefathers, covering customs, festivals, art, music, religion and science.
ref: Lesson 1: India's Cultural and Natural Heritage

add: NOT SCIENCE: sort examples of culture into physical and non-physical parts; add to a culture unit.
point: Culture has a physical side (costumes, food, household goods) and a non-physical side (ideas, ideals, feelings, beliefs).
ref: Lesson 1: India's Cultural and Natural Heritage

add: NOT SCIENCE: culture is learnt, changes over time and varies by region; add to a culture unit.
point: Culture is learnt, builds up across generations, keeps changing, and varies with religion, caste and region.
ref: Lesson 1: India's Cultural and Natural Heritage

add: NOT SCIENCE: why culture matters for how we think and live; add to a culture unit.
point: Culture shapes who we are: it makes us social beings, teaches how to live, and links faith with everyday life.
ref: Lesson 1: India's Cultural and Natural Heritage

add: NOT SCIENCE: name heritage sites (Taj Mahal, Qutub Minar, Golden Temple) and where they stand; planned in sci.india.heritage.L5.
point: Cultural heritage means monuments and works inherited from the past, such as the Taj Mahal, Qutub Minar and the Golden Temple.
ref: Lesson 1: India's Cultural and Natural Heritage

evidence: Aryabhata's boat: an idea from India, 499 CE
point: Our literature, scriptures, scientific discoveries and the work of early scholars like Aryabhatta are also part of our legacy.
ref: Lesson 1: India's Cultural and Natural Heritage

add: NOT SCIENCE: heritage damaged by weather, pollution and people, and what citizens can do; planned in sci.india.heritage.L5.
point: Heritage sites are damaged by weather, pollution, tourists writing on walls and people living in them; everyone must help protect them.
ref: Lesson 1: India's Cultural and Natural Heritage

evidence: The Thar desert is one ecological region
add: Add the list of natural heritage (forests, mountains, seas, deserts, minerals) and why to use them with care.
point: India's natural heritage includes plants, animals, forests, mountains, rivers, seas, deserts and minerals, which must be used with care.
ref: Lesson 1: India's Cultural and Natural Heritage

evidence: The wet forest of the Western Ghats is another
add: Add the share of India under forest, forest products (wood, lac, rubber) and forest benefits (rain, soil).
point: Forests cover about a fifth of India, give wood, herbs, rubber, lac and silk, bring rain and prevent erosion; tree types vary by region.
ref: Lesson 1: India's Cultural and Natural Heritage

add: Add India's bird and animal counts by region, and the national parks that protect them.
point: India has many animal species and more than 1200 bird species; regions differ, and 55 national parks protect wildlife.
ref: Lesson 1: India's Cultural and Natural Heritage

add: Add Himalayan rivers (Ganga, Brahmaputra) feeding the plains, and peninsular rivers (Krishna, Cauvery) irrigating the land.
point: Himalayan rivers such as the Ganga and Brahmaputra feed the northern plains, while southern rivers such as the Krishna and Cauvery irrigate the peninsula.
ref: Lesson 1: India's Cultural and Natural Heritage

add: Add to the planned Earth's rocks unit: minerals like iron, coal and bauxite, mining, refining, and imported petroleum.
point: Minerals such as iron, coal, bauxite and petroleum are dug from the earth, refined, and used as fuel and in industry; petroleum is partly imported.
ref: Lesson 1: India's Cultural and Natural Heritage

add: NOT SCIENCE: India's castes, religions and languages, and unity in diversity; planned in sci.india.unity-in-diversity.L5.
point: India has many castes, communities, religions and languages, yet national identity comes first.
ref: Lesson 2: Peace, Unity and Harmony in Indian Society

add: NOT SCIENCE: tribes (Adivasis), their customs and constitutional support; planned in sci.india.unity-in-diversity.L5.
point: Tribes (Adivasis) keep their own customs, religions and ways of living, and the Constitution gives them reservation.
ref: Lesson 2: Peace, Unity and Harmony in Indian Society

add: NOT SCIENCE: how trade and settlers mixed culture, art and food across states; planned in sci.india.unity-in-diversity.L5.
point: Cultures mixed through trade and settlers from abroad, enriching art, food, dress and festivals across states.
ref: Lesson 2: Peace, Unity and Harmony in Indian Society

evidence: I can name festivals from different parts of India, and give a food, a dress or a custom for each one
point: Festivals like Makar Sankranti, Bihu, Pongal and Onam show local variety within shared celebration.
ref: Lesson 2: Peace, Unity and Harmony in Indian Society

evidence: Gandhi led millions of people in the freedom struggle without violence
point: The freedom struggle and national symbols such as the flag, anthem and constitution build a sense of national unity.
ref: Lesson 2: Peace, Unity and Harmony in Indian Society

add: NOT SCIENCE: peace in homes and nations, and settling disputes by dialogue; add to a civics or values unit.
point: Peace in homes, villages and countries brings development, while conflict wastes strength and money; disputes should be settled by talking.
ref: Lesson 2: Peace, Unity and Harmony in Indian Society

add: NOT SCIENCE: define harmony and show how the law treats all citizens equally; extend sci.family.family.L3.
point: Harmony means equality without high or low status, and the law treats all citizens as equal.
ref: Lesson 2: Peace, Unity and Harmony in Indian Society

add: NOT SCIENCE: Ashoka after the Kalinga war, Dhamma officers and rock edicts; add to planned sci.india.unity-in-diversity.L5.
point: Emperor Ashoka turned to Buddhist ideas after the Kalinga war, sent Dhamma officers and carved messages on rocks and pillars.
ref: Lesson 2: Peace, Unity and Harmony in Indian Society

add: NOT SCIENCE: Ashoka's respect for all faiths, kindness and charity; add to planned sci.india.unity-in-diversity.L5.
point: Ashoka's teaching: respect for all faiths, kindness to servants and animals, respect for elders and charity.
ref: Lesson 2: Peace, Unity and Harmony in Indian Society

add: NOT SCIENCE: Akbar's Sulh-i-Kul, Din-i-Ilahi and building peace between Hindus and Muslims; add to planned sci.india.unity-in-diversity.L5.
point: Emperor Akbar promoted brotherhood by honouring Hindu scholars, marrying a Rajput princess and starting Sulh-i-Kul and Din-i-Ilahi.
ref: Lesson 2: Peace, Unity and Harmony in Indian Society

add: NOT SCIENCE: social issues (big families, women's low education, dowry, female foeticide) that slow progress; add to planned sci.india.government-and-rights.L5.
point: Social issues such as big families, low education of women, dowry and female foeticide slow down a society's progress.
ref: Lesson 3: Our Social Issues

add: NOT SCIENCE: costs, nutrition and attention in large families; add to a family unit (sci.family.family.L3 does not cover it).
point: A large family often faces higher costs, poor nutrition, little attention to each child, and more poverty and tension.
ref: Lesson 3: Our Social Issues

add: NOT SCIENCE: how a small family can give love, balanced food and education; add to a family unit.
point: A small family can give children more love, balanced food and education, and keeps the mother healthy.
ref: Lesson 3: Our Social Issues

add: NOT SCIENCE: learning starts at home and the family is the first school; add to a family unit.
point: Education means gaining knowledge in any way, not only reading and writing, and the family is a child's first school.
ref: Lesson 3: Our Social Issues

add: NOT SCIENCE: why education brings jobs, self-confidence and freedom from superstition; add to a family or civics unit.
point: Education brings jobs, better decisions, self-confidence, awareness of rights and duties, and removes superstition and social evils.
ref: Lesson 3: Our Social Issues

evidence: I can give examples of how girls and women were kept out of school
point: Girls' education was neglected through history; women's literacy was very low at independence and many girls still miss school.
ref: Lesson 3: Our Social Issues

add: NOT SCIENCE: causes of women's unequal status (dependence, dowry, purdah, illiteracy); extend sci.family.family.L3.
point: Women's inequality has causes: family customs, economic dependence, male-dominated decisions, illiteracy, poverty, large families and wrong attitudes.
ref: Lesson 3: Our Social Issues

add: NOT SCIENCE: progress for women (literacy programmes, panchayat seats, public life); extend sci.family.family.L3.
point: Progress for women includes literacy programmes, one-third reservation in panchayats, more women at work and in public life.
ref: Lesson 3: Our Social Issues

add: NOT SCIENCE: women's legal rights (marriage age, stri-dhan, maintenance, property); extend sci.family.family.L3.
point: Women have legal rights: marriage at 18, keeping their own name, controlling stri-dhan, custody and maintenance after divorce, and a share of property.
ref: Lesson 3: Our Social Issues

add: NOT SCIENCE: Domestic Violence Act 2001 and the 1994 pre-natal sex test law; extend sci.family.family.L3.
point: Laws protect women: the Domestic Violence Act 2001, the 1994 law against finding a baby's sex before birth, and court help for deserted wives.
ref: Lesson 3: Our Social Issues

add: NOT SCIENCE: how a dowry gift became a harmful demand, and its causes; extend sci.family.family.L3.
point: Dowry began as a gift given willingly, but became a demand that spreads through wealth, caste limits, social show and costly education.
ref: Lesson 3: Our Social Issues

add: NOT SCIENCE: harms of dowry (debt, harassment, mismatched marriage, deaths); extend sci.family.family.L3.
point: Dowry causes debt, forced or mismatched marriages, harassment, suicide among girls, and more unmarried girls from poor families.
ref: Lesson 3: Our Social Issues

add: NOT SCIENCE: 1961 Dowry Prohibition Act, dowry death and the stri-dhan list; add to a civics unit.
point: Dowry is illegal under the 1961 Prohibition of Dowry Act; a death within seven years of marriage after dowry harassment is dowry death.
ref: Lesson 3: Our Social Issues

add: NOT SCIENCE: pre-British spice and cloth trade, European traders and the Mughal decline; planned in sci.india.freedom-struggle.L5.
point: Before British rule, India's spice and cloth trade drew European traders, and the Mughal empire weakened after Aurangzeb died in 1707.
ref: Lesson 4: Our Freedom Struggle

add: NOT SCIENCE: East India Company's monopoly, Battle of Plassey 1757 and the order of British expansion; planned in sci.india.freedom-struggle.L5.
point: The English East India Company gained trade monopoly and then political power after the Battle of Plassey in 1757.
ref: Lesson 4: Our Freedom Struggle

add: NOT SCIENCE: British rules that harmed farmers (indigo, opium) and traders; planned in sci.india.freedom-struggle.L5.
point: British rule exploited farmers, who were forced to grow opium and indigo, and blocked Indian factories and free trade.
ref: Lesson 4: Our Freedom Struggle

add: NOT SCIENCE: Haider Ali and Tipu Sultan's resistance, and the annexation of Oudh and Jhansi; planned in sci.india.freedom-struggle.L5.
point: Haider Ali and Tipu Sultan of Mysore resisted the British, and the British also took over kingdoms such as Oudh and Jhansi.
ref: Lesson 4: Our Freedom Struggle

add: NOT SCIENCE: causes, spread and result of the 1857 revolt; planned in sci.india.freedom-struggle.L5.
point: The 1857 revolt began with Mangal Pandey and spread across North India, joined by kings, soldiers and common people, but failed; British Crown rule followed.
ref: Lesson 4: Our Freedom Struggle

add: NOT SCIENCE: Congress moderates and radicals before Gandhi; planned in sci.india.freedom-struggle.L5.
point: The Indian National Congress, founded in 1885, split into moderates and radicals before Gandhi took the lead of the movement.
ref: Lesson 4: Our Freedom Struggle

add: NOT SCIENCE: Gandhi's methods (Ahimsa, Satyagraha, Dandi March, Quit India) with an example each; extend sci.india.national-identity.L3.
point: Gandhiji's methods were non-violence (Ahimsa), non-cooperation, Satyagraha at Champaran, the Dandi salt march and the Quit India movement.
ref: Lesson 4: Our Freedom Struggle

add: NOT SCIENCE: Jallianwala Bagh 1919 and its effect on revolutionaries; planned in sci.india.freedom-struggle.L5.
point: Massacre at Jallianwala Bagh in 1919 made people angry and strengthened revolutionaries such as Bhagat Singh and Chandrashekhar Azad.
ref: Lesson 4: Our Freedom Struggle

add: NOT SCIENCE: freedom leaders (Nehru, Bose, Patel, Azad, Sarojini Naidu) and their regions; planned in sci.india.freedom-struggle.L5.
point: Many leaders joined the struggle, including Nehru, Bose, Patel, Azad, Sarojini Naidu and Rajendra Prasad, from all regions and communities.
ref: Lesson 4: Our Freedom Struggle

add: NOT SCIENCE: 15 August 1947, the long struggle and why freedom must be protected; extend sci.india.national-identity.L3.
point: India became free on 15 August 1947; freedom was won by long struggle and many sacrifices, so it must be protected.
ref: Lesson 4: Our Freedom Struggle

add: NOT SCIENCE: India's neighbours, seas and place in Asia; add to a planned map unit (sci.planet-earth.maps-and-directions.L5).
point: India is the seventh largest country, lies in Asia, has neighbours on its land borders, and is washed by three seas.
ref: Lesson 5: The States of India and their Physical Features

add: NOT SCIENCE: India's 29 states, 7 union territories and capitals; planned in sci.india.states-and-features.L5.
point: India has 29 states and 7 union territories, each with a capital; Delhi is the national capital.
ref: Lesson 5: The States of India and their Physical Features

add: Add the equator and Tropic of Cancer as reference lines for locating places.
point: The equator, hemispheres, Tropic of Cancer and lines of latitude and longitude are used to locate places on a globe.
ref: Lesson 5: The States of India and their Physical Features

add: Add India's six physical divisions and locate each on a map.
point: India has six physical divisions: northern mountains, northern plains, peninsular plateau, Thar desert, coastal plains and islands.
ref: Lesson 5: The States of India and their Physical Features

add: Add the Himalayan ranges, Mount Everest, passes and the rivers they feed.
point: The Himalayas run from Kashmir to Arunachal Pradesh, contain the world's highest peak, and feed many rivers and hill stations.
ref: Lesson 5: The States of India and their Physical Features

add: Add how Indus, Ganga and Brahmaputra soils built the fertile northern plains; Harappa.
point: The northern plains are built from soil of the Indus, Ganga and Brahmaputra, are very fertile, and hosted ancient cities such as Harappa.
ref: Lesson 5: The States of India and their Physical Features

add: Add the Central Highlands and the volcanic Deccan Plateau with its black soil.
point: The peninsular plateau has the Central Highlands, north of the Narmada, and the Deccan Plateau, formed by volcanic eruption, with black soil.
ref: Lesson 5: The States of India and their Physical Features

add: Add the Western and Eastern Ghats and which rivers flow east or west across the plateau.
point: The Western and Eastern Ghats border the plateau, with passes and rivers; the Godavari, Krishna and Cauvery flow to the Bay of Bengal.
ref: Lesson 5: The States of India and their Physical Features

add: Add the Thar Desert's thorny bushes and why the Luni river disappears in sand.
point: The Thar Desert, to the west of the Aravalli, has thorny bushes, and its river Luni disappears in the sand except in the rains.
ref: Lesson 5: The States of India and their Physical Features

add: Add coastal plains beside both seas and the Andaman and Lakshadweep island groups.
point: Coastal plains lie beside both seas; the Andaman and Nicobar and Lakshadweep island groups are in the Bay of Bengal and Arabian Sea.
ref: Lesson 5: The States of India and their Physical Features

add: Add climate as weather over 30 years, and how latitude, sea, height and winds shape it.
point: Climate, the weather over 30 years or more, depends on latitude, distance from sea, height, mountains and wind direction.
ref: Lesson 5: The States of India and their Physical Features

add: Add the four crop groups (food, cash, plantation, horticulture) and what each needs.
point: Crops are grouped as food, cash, plantation and horticulture crops, and each needs its own soil, rainfall and temperature.
ref: Lesson 5: The States of India and their Physical Features

evidence: The wet forest of the Western Ghats is another
add: Add forest types by rainfall (evergreen, deciduous, thorn, mangrove, Himalayan) and their typical trees.
