point: Forests differ with rainfall: evergreen, deciduous (moist and dry), thorn, mangrove and Himalayan forests each have typical trees.
ref: Lesson 5: The States of India and their Physical Features

add: NOT SCIENCE: the three arms of government (Legislature, Executive, Judiciary); planned in sci.india.government-and-rights.L5.
point: Government has three parts: the Legislature makes laws, the Executive runs administration, and the Judiciary protects the Constitution and laws.
ref: Lesson 6: Our Community and Public Administration

add: NOT SCIENCE: define democracy; the 1950 Constitution date is in sci.india.national-identity.L3, add the definition to government-and-rights.L5.
point: Democracy means government of the people, by the people and for the people; the Constitution took effect on 26 January 1950.
ref: Lesson 6: Our Community and Public Administration

add: NOT SCIENCE: who may vote (18+, name on voters list) and why each vote matters; extend sci.india.government-and-rights.L3.
point: Every citizen aged 18 or above whose name is on the voters list can vote, and every vote matters even though turnout is low.
ref: Lesson 6: Our Community and Public Administration

add: NOT SCIENCE: Lok Sabha's members, five-year term and how the Prime Minister is chosen; planned in sci.india.government-and-rights.L5.
point: Parliament has two houses; the Lok Sabha has up to 545 members elected directly for five years, and the majority party's leader becomes Prime Minister.
ref: Lesson 6: Our Community and Public Administration

add: NOT SCIENCE: Rajya Sabha's indirect election and six-year terms, compared with the Lok Sabha; planned in sci.india.government-and-rights.L5.
point: The Rajya Sabha has 250 members, 12 nominated, elected indirectly by state legislators, is never dissolved, and has six-year terms.
ref: Lesson 6: Our Community and Public Administration

add: NOT SCIENCE: the President as constitutional head and who really governs; planned in sci.india.government-and-rights.L5.
point: The President is the constitutional head; the Prime Minister and the cabinet exercise real executive power, and the Governor heads a state's executive.
ref: Lesson 6: Our Community and Public Administration

add: NOT SCIENCE: the Supreme Court's role, fundamental rights and binding rulings; planned in sci.india.government-and-rights.L5.
point: The Supreme Court is the highest court; its rulings bind all courts and it protects fundamental rights.
ref: Lesson 6: Our Community and Public Administration

add: NOT SCIENCE: how powers are shared between Centre and states in India's federal system; planned in sci.india.government-and-rights.L5.
point: India is a federal system in which Centre and states have separate powers; in a clash, the Centre's law prevails.
ref: Lesson 6: Our Community and Public Administration

add: NOT SCIENCE: Gram Sabha, Panches, Sarpanch and women's one-third seats in a Panchayat; extend sci.india.government-and-rights.L3.
point: A village Panchayat has a Gram Sabha, a committee of 9 to 15 Panches, and a Sarpanch; one-third of seats are reserved for women.
ref: Lesson 6: Our Community and Public Administration

add: NOT SCIENCE: Gram Sabha meeting dates and removal of a village head by no-confidence; planned in sci.india.government-and-rights.L5.
point: Gram Sabha meets on 26 January, 1 May, 15 August and 2 October; a two-thirds no-confidence motion can remove the village head.
ref: Lesson 6: Our Community and Public Administration

add: NOT SCIENCE: duties of village Panchayats (lighting, water, health, pensions, fair price shops); planned in sci.india.government-and-rights.L5.
point: Panchayats look after lighting, clean water, birth and death registration, health, pensions, fair price shops, trees and village industries.
ref: Lesson 6: Our Community and Public Administration

add: NOT SCIENCE: block and district Panchayats and their five-year plans; planned in sci.india.government-and-rights.L5.
point: Block and district Panchayats are formed from village Panchayats and plan development for their areas for five years.
ref: Lesson 6: Our Community and Public Administration

add: NOT SCIENCE: City Councils, Municipal Councils and Municipal Corporations with a Mayor; planned in sci.india.government-and-rights.L5.
point: Cities have City Councils, Municipal Councils (population 3 to 5 lakh, minimum age 25) and Municipal Corporations (above 5 lakh, with a Mayor).
ref: Lesson 6: Our Community and Public Administration

add: NOT SCIENCE: local bodies' taxes and state grants for city services; planned in sci.india.government-and-rights.L5.
point: Local bodies raise money through taxes and receive grants from state governments to pay for city services.
ref: Lesson 6: Our Community and Public Administration

evidence: Who eats whom: simple food chains starting with plants
point: Plants and animals depend on each other, and all animals depend on plants for food.
ref: Lesson 7: Life of Plants and Animals

evidence: Carbon dioxide in, oxygen out
point: Green plants make food with sunlight, water and carbon dioxide in photosynthesis, releasing oxygen that keeps air balanced.
ref: Lesson 7: Life of Plants and Animals

evidence: Some birds and bats are pollinators, though they are not insects
add: Add trees as shelter for birds and other animals, with one example.
point: Trees give shelter to birds and animals, and insects and birds carry pollen from flower to flower during pollination.
ref: Lesson 7: Life of Plants and Animals

evidence: How seeds travel: wings and wind, water, animals and people
add: Add animal dispersal: seeds eaten in fruit and passed in dung, and seeds that stick to fur.
point: Animals spread seeds by eating fruit and passing seeds in dung, and some seeds stick to fur and fall far away.
ref: Lesson 7: Life of Plants and Animals

evidence: Food webs: what happens when one link disappears
point: A food chain shows who eats whom, such as grass, deer, lion; many linked chains form a food web, called a food trap.
ref: Lesson 7: Life of Plants and Animals

evidence: A herbivore eats plants. A carnivore eats other animals. An omnivore eats both.
point: Animals are herbivores (eat plants), carnivores (eat meat), omnivores (eat both) or scavengers (eat dead animals).
ref: Lesson 7: Life of Plants and Animals

evidence: Decomposers: how worms, moulds and bacteria turn dead things into soil
point: Bacteria break down dead plants and animals and mix them into the soil, which recycles nutrients.
ref: Lesson 7: Life of Plants and Animals

evidence: With no predators, the herbivores increase until they eat down the plants.
point: Natural balance depends on predators controlling plant-eaters; without them, plant-eaters multiply and destroy vegetation.
ref: Lesson 7: Life of Plants and Animals

add: Add how cutting forests reduces rain, raises flood and drought risk, and adds carbon dioxide to the air.
point: Cutting forests destroys habitats, reduces rain, raises the risk of floods and drought, and adds carbon dioxide to the air.
ref: Lesson 7: Life of Plants and Animals

evidence: A Bishnoi woman, Amrita Devi, held on to a tree
add: Add two protections: permission before felling, and planting saplings to replace trees.
point: Forests are protected by permission before felling and by planting saplings, as in the Bishnoi community's example.
ref: Lesson 7: Life of Plants and Animals

evidence: Cutting trees and hunting are not allowed there
add: Add the measures: hunting ban, no animal-skin goods, and what sanctuaries and national parks are for.
point: Animals are protected by stopping hunting, avoiding articles made from animal skin, and creating national parks and sanctuaries.
ref: Lesson 7: Life of Plants and Animals

evidence: Every harvest carries nutrients away from the field
point: Soil is the basis of life; cereals, fruits, flowers and herbs grow in it, so the harvest depends on the soil.
ref: Lesson 8: Soil and Crops

evidence: Small dark bits float on top
point: Stirring soil in water and letting it settle shows floating humus; humus makes soil soft and fertile, and the top layer is richest.
ref: Lesson 8: Soil and Crops

evidence: I can explain why sand drains fast, clay holds water
add: Add which crops suit clay soil (rice, sugarcane) and which suit sandy soil (groundnut, melon, potato).
point: Clay soil holds water for long and suits cotton, rice, sugarcane and gram; sandy soil drains fast and suits groundnut, melon and potato.
ref: Lesson 8: Soil and Crops

evidence: rainy places, such as the laterite soils of Kerala tend to be acidic
add: Add alluvial soil as the mix suited to most crops, and lime and gypsum to treat acidic soil.
point: Alluvial soil is a mix suited to most crops, while acidic soil is infertile and can be improved with lime and gypsum.
ref: Lesson 8: Soil and Crops

evidence: A rice plant makes their food in their leaves, using sunlight
add: Add why crops must be sown on time to germinate well and give a good yield.
point: Crops need water, air, sunlight and nutrients, and must be sown on time to germinate well and give a good yield.
ref: Lesson 8: Soil and Crops

add: Add the squeeze-and-crumble lump test to check whether a moist field is ready for tilling.
point: Before tilling, dig a lump and squeeze it: if it crumbles the moist field is ready; if not, the field is still raw.
ref: Lesson 8: Soil and Crops

add: Add seed treatment against disease, and bio-fertilisers, for even germination.
point: Seed treatment with chemicals or bio-fertilisers protects seeds from disease and makes germination uniform.
ref: Lesson 8: Soil and Crops

evidence: It also lets weeds be ploughed in
add: Add that weeds steal water and nutrients, and that timely weeding and right watering protect crops.
point: Weeds steal water and nutrients, so timely weeding, hoeing and correct irrigation keep crops healthy; too much water harms them.
ref: Lesson 8: Soil and Crops

evidence: The Soil Health Card is a report on a soil test
point: Fertiliser should be used after soil is tested; organic manure such as compost, cow dung and green manure improves soil and food.
ref: Lesson 8: Soil and Crops

evidence: A pesticide is a poison used to kill insects who eat crops
add: Add crop damage by pests and neel gai, and safe organic treatments for farmers.
point: Pests, diseases and animals such as neel gai and monkeys damage crops, so farmers must watch and use safe organic treatments.
ref: Lesson 8: Soil and Crops

add: Add harvest timing, sorting, sun-drying grain and safe storage.
point: Harvest at the right ripeness, sort and dry the grain in sun until crisp, then store it.
ref: Lesson 8: Soil and Crops

add: Add rabi, kharif and zayyad crops with their sowing and harvest months.
point: Rabi crops are sown in November-December; kharif crops in July-August; zayyad crops fill the gap from March to June.
ref: Lesson 8: Soil and Crops

add: Add a sowing test with ten seeds per crop, and the causes of plant failure.
point: Sow ten seeds each of several crops in beds, care for them, and use the results to think about soil, weather and other causes.
ref: Lesson 8: Soil and Crops

evidence: heavy rain washes bare soil away, and strong wind blows dry soil away. This is called soil erosion
point: Soil erosion is the wearing away of the fertile top layer by rain water and wind, which lowers crop yield.
ref: Lesson 9: Conservation of Soil and Forests (part, to book page 142)

evidence: heavy rain washes bare soil away, and strong wind blows dry soil away
add: Add gullies and ravines cut by fast rain water, and wind erosion in dry areas.
point: Rain erosion forms gullies and ravines when water flows fast in channels, while wind erosion is common in dry and arid areas.
ref: Lesson 9: Conservation of Soil and Forests (part, to book page 142)

evidence: New soil forms very slowly, and soil can be lost quickly by erosion
add: Add the harms of erosion: silted wells and canals, floods, lost pasture and farm income.
point: Eroded soil reduces water in wells and rivers, blocks canals, causes floods, reduces pasture and lowers farm income.
ref: Lesson 9: Conservation of Soil and Forests (part, to book page 142)

evidence: Terraces or bunds across the slope, mulch between the rows, plants whose roots hold the soil
point: On slopes, boundary walls (dolbandi), embankments with outlets and terrace farming stop soil from being washed away.
ref: Lesson 9: Conservation of Soil and Forests (part, to book page 142)

evidence: Roots hold the soil, and plants slow the rain
add: Add check dams with outlets on slopes, rivers and drains that slow water and cut erosion.
point: Planting grass, shrubs and trees holds soil roots in place, and check dams with outlets slow water on rivers and drains.
ref: Lesson 9: Conservation of Soil and Forests (part, to book page 142)

add: Add soil pollution from non-rotting waste, pesticides and factory waste, and why it harms crops.
point: Soil pollution is caused by non-rotting waste like polythene and glass, chemical pesticides and fertilisers, and factory waste.
ref: Lesson 9: Conservation of Soil and Forests (part, to book page 142)

add: Add controls on factory discharge, organic pest sprays and manure as prevention.
point: Soil pollution is cut by sorting and recycling waste, stopping factory discharge, and using organic pest sprays and manure.
ref: Lesson 9: Conservation of Soil and Forests (part, to book page 142)

evidence: so your brain has fuel while you sleep
point: Energy is the power or capacity to do work, and we need it for every activity, even sleeping, because the lungs and heart keep working.
ref: Level B, Lesson 10: Sources of Energy and their Importance, p.150-151

point: Non-renewable energy sources (coal, kerosene, cooking gas, petrol, diesel) finish once they are used, so they cannot be used again and again.
ref: Level B, Lesson 10: Sources of Energy and their Importance, p.151

add: DATED: reserve years (30-35, up to 100) are old estimates; teach limited fuel stocks and changing estimates in sci.energy.sources-and-saving.L5.
point: The book estimates that oil and gas reserves will last about 30 to 35 years and coal up to 100 years at current and future use.
ref: Level B, Lesson 10: Sources of Energy and their Importance, p.152

evidence: do not run out
point: Renewable energy sources never finish; the book names wind, water and sunlight, and says food gives us energy that nature provides again and again.
ref: Level B, Lesson 10: Sources of Energy and their Importance, p.152

evidence: follow an energy chain back to the Sun
point: Food energy is the energy we get from food; all living beings depend on plants, which make their own food from sunlight.
ref: Level B, Lesson 10: Sources of Energy and their Importance, p.153

evidence: Solar panels on a roof make clean energy.
add: Add solar uses: drying grain and clothes, solar cooker, water heater, solar cells for bulbs and small vehicles.
point: Solar energy comes from the sun as light and heat and is used to dry clothes and grain, cook, heat water, light bulbs and run small vehicles.
ref: Level B, Lesson 10: Sources of Energy and their Importance, p.153-154

evidence: Almost all food starts with caught sunlight
point: The sun never runs out of energy, so it is called a source of energy; life on earth and the growth of crops depend on its light, and sunlight gives us Vitamin D.
ref: Level B, Lesson 10: Sources of Energy and their Importance, p.153-154

evidence: wind and flowing water make electricity without smoke
add: Add windmills that pump well water and grind flour, and pinwheels as moving-air examples.
point: Wind energy is moving air doing work: it spins pinwheels, and in windy places windmills pump water from wells, make electricity and grind flour.
ref: Level B, Lesson 10: Sources of Energy and their Importance, p.154

evidence: flowing water make electricity without smoke
point: Hydro energy is the energy of flowing water; hydro power stations use flowing water to make electricity, just as flowing water carries floating logs.
ref: Level B, Lesson 10: Sources of Energy and their Importance, p.154

evidence: what rots, what stays
add: Add biogas: dung, dead leaves and crop waste in a biogas plant give cooking gas and leftover manure.
point: Organic (biogas) energy comes from dung, dead animals, dry leaves and crop waste put into a biogas plant; the gas cooks food and gives light, and the leftover is used as manure.
ref: Level B, Lesson 10: Sources of Energy and their Importance, p.155

evidence: A fan needs electricity.
point: Electrical energy is the energy of electricity, used to light bulbs and run fans, tubewells, radios, televisions, computers, fridges and trains.
ref: Level B, Lesson 10: Sources of Energy and their Importance, p.155

evidence: A magnet attracts
add: Add magnets pulling iron from scrap, cranes lifting iron, and an electric bell.
point: Magnetic energy is the pull of a magnet on iron; it separates iron from scrap, lifts heavy iron products and works inside an electric bell.
ref: Level B, Lesson 10: Sources of Energy and their Importance, p.155-156

evidence: The Sun, food, fuel, electricity, wind and flowing water are sources of energy we use every day.
add: Book lists seven kinds; magnetism and biogas are not standard energy types. Say so, and name the six sources here.
point: There are seven kinds of energy: food, solar, wind, hydro, organic, electrical and magnetic.
ref: Level B, Lesson 10: Sources of Energy and their Importance, p.156

point: Because coal, petrol and kerosene are running low, we should use more alternative sources: solar cookers, windmills, electricity and biogas.
ref: Level B, Lesson 10: Sources of Energy and their Importance, p.156

evidence: use less, and choose cleaner
point: Energy saving matters because falling fuel stocks can cause an energy crisis, and every household can help by saving energy.
ref: Level B, Lesson 10: Sources of Energy and their Importance, p.157

evidence: Switch off fans and lights in empty rooms.
point: At home, switch off bulbs, tubes and fans when not needed, close taps (water supply uses energy), and cover utensils while cooking.
ref: Level B, Lesson 10: Sources of Energy and their Importance, p.157

evidence: Put a lid on the pot.
add: Add cooking savings: soak rice and pulses, use only the water needed, and cook in a pressure cooker.
point: In cooking, use only the water needed, soak rice and pulses before cooking, and use a pressure cooker instead of an open pan.
ref: Level B, Lesson 10: Sources of Energy and their Importance, p.157

point: Use efficient appliances and transport: CFL bulbs or tube lights instead of normal bulbs, and public transport instead of personal vehicles.
ref: Level B, Lesson 10: Sources of Energy and their Importance, p.157

add: Add a solar cooker build (box, black paper, glass cover, foil reflector, food cooking in sunlight) to sci.energy.sources-and-saving.L5.
point: A solar cooker can be made from a wooden or card-board box with black paper inside and outside, a glass cover, and a mirror or aluminium foil reflecting sunlight into the box.
ref: Level B, Lesson 10: Sources of Energy and their Importance, p.161

evidence: name the eight planets in order
point: The sun is a star, and planets are celestial bodies that go round the sun; the book names eight planets of the solar system.
ref: Level B, Lesson 11: Solar System and Earth, p.163

evidence: The Sun is the star nearest to us.
point: The sun looks bigger than other stars because it is the star closest to the earth.
ref: Level B, Lesson 11: Solar System and Earth, p.163

evidence: it is the only world where we know living beings exist
point: Earth is the only planet with life, because it has air and water; it is round (geoid or spherical) and has a North Pole and a South Pole.
ref: Level B, Lesson 11: Solar System and Earth, p.163

evidence: spins once in 23 hours 56 minutes
point: Rotation is the earth turning on its axis, and one full rotation takes 24 hours.
ref: Level B, Lesson 11: Solar System and Earth, p.163

evidence: about 365 days and 6 hours
point: Revolution is the earth moving round the sun on a fixed path called an orbit, taking 365 days and 6 hours; the earth is slightly tilted on its axis.
ref: Level B, Lesson 11: Solar System and Earth, p.163

evidence: takes about 29 and a half days
point: A celestial body that moves round a star is a planet, and one that moves round a planet is a satellite; the moon is the earth's satellite and takes 29 and a half days to go round the earth.
ref: Level B, Lesson 11: Solar System and Earth, p.164

evidence: The Moon makes no light.
point: The moon has no light of its own; the lit part changes through the month, from full moon (purnima) to new moon (amavasya), and this is called the phases of the moon.
ref: Level B, Lesson 11: Solar System and Earth, p.164-165

evidence: explain the Moon's phases and the two pakshas
point: The Indian calendar counts dates by the moon: each month has two 15-day fortnights, Shukla Paksha (new moon to full moon) and Krishna Paksha (full moon to new moon); zodiac cycles and horoscopes come from star groups.
ref: Level B, Lesson 11: Solar System and Earth, p.164-165

evidence: tell a natural satellite from an artificial one
point: Natural satellites (such as the moon) move round planets, while artificial satellites are man-made machines that orbit the earth.
ref: Level B, Lesson 11: Solar System and Earth, p.165

evidence: INSAT weather satellite stays in one place
add: Add satellite jobs: spotting forest fires and relaying TV signals between countries.
point: Artificial satellites take pictures of the earth used for weather forecasts and spotting forest fires, and carry TV signals so that events in one country are seen in another.
ref: Level B, Lesson 11: Solar System and Earth, p.165

point: Imaginary latitude lines run East to West and help locate places; the equator is the central latitude (0 degrees) and divides the earth into Northern and Southern hemispheres.
ref: Level B, Lesson 11: Solar System and Earth, p.166

evidence: Arctic Circle
point: Four important latitude lines are the Tropic of Cancer and the Tropic of Capricorn (23 and a half degrees North and South) and the Arctic and Antarctic Circles (66 and a half degrees North and South).
ref: Level B, Lesson 11: Solar System and Earth, p.166

point: Longitude lines run North to South, meet at the poles, number 360, and the Meridian (0 degrees) divides the earth into Eastern and Western hemispheres.
ref: Level B, Lesson 11: Solar System and Earth, p.167

point: Time differs by about 4 minutes between two longitude lines, and the time of all countries is worked out from the 0 degree line that passes through Greenwich in England.
ref: Level B, Lesson 11: Solar System and Earth, p.168

add: Add India standard time from 82.5 E. Allahabad is an old name; the city is now Prayagraj.
point: India has one Standard time, taken from the 82 and a half degree East longitude line which passes through Allahabad, so that the whole country keeps the same time.
ref: Level B, Lesson 11: Solar System and Earth, p.168

evidence: most near the poles
add: Add: poles have six months of day and six months of night, kept cold by slanting rays.
point: Because the earth is tilted, day and night are not equal everywhere: they are equal all year on the equator, and at the poles there is six months of day and six months of night, with slanting sun rays that keep the poles cold.
ref: Level B, Lesson 11: Solar System and Earth, p.168

evidence: One is about 21 June
point: On 21 June the sun is overhead at the Tropic of Cancer, so the Northern Hemisphere has its longest day, and on 22 December the sun is overhead at the Tropic of Capricorn, giving the Southern Hemisphere long days.
ref: Level B, Lesson 11: Solar System and Earth, p.169

evidence: name the two solstices and the two equinoxes, give their dates
point: On 21 March and 23 September the sun shines directly on the equator, so days and nights are equal everywhere; these are the Spring and Autumn Equinox.
ref: Level B, Lesson 11: Solar System and Earth, p.169

evidence: The Earth is nearest to the Sun in early January
point: The earth is closest to the sun (perihelion) on 3 January and farthest (aphelion) on 4 July; the book says the distance from the sun causes changes in temperature and seasons.
ref: Level B, Lesson 11: Solar System and Earth, p.170

evidence: protective foods
point: Food contains nutrients that do different jobs: carbohydrates and fats give strength, proteins help the body grow, and vitamins and mineral salts protect us from disease.
ref: Level B, Lesson 12: Food and Health, p.175

evidence: looks pale
add: Add anaemia signs: yellow gums, white nails, swelling of face and feet, fast heartbeat in severe cases.
point: Anaemia happens when blood becomes thin, usually from lack of iron; its signs are pale skin, yellow gums, white nails, tiredness, and in severe cases face and feet swelling and a fast heartbeat.
ref: Level B, Lesson 12: Food and Health, p.176

evidence: Ragi dosa with sambar
point: To prevent anaemia, eat iron-rich food such as bajra, ragi, jaggery, spinach, meat, fish, chicken and eggs, and take iron tablets with a doctor's advice if it gets worse.
ref: Level B, Lesson 12: Food and Health, p.176

evidence: Kwashiorkor often begins after a child stops breastfeeding
point: Kwashiorkor, sometimes called wet malnutrition, affects children with too little protein: swollen face, stopped growth, swelling of hands and feet, and loss of colour in skin and hair.
ref: Level B, Lesson 12: Food and Health, p.176-177

evidence: dal with rice, roasted chana
point: A child with kwashiorkor needs extra protein foods, given in greater quantity and at least three meals a day with light snacks in between.
ref: Level B, Lesson 12: Food and Health, p.176-177

evidence: A serious kind of malnutrition from too little food
point: Rickets from too little food (called dry malnutrition) makes children lose great weight, look like old people, have a protruding stomach and skin over bones; it is treated with large amounts of nutritious food.
ref: Level B, Lesson 12: Food and Health, p.177

evidence: Vitamin D is the exception, because skin makes it in sunlight.
add: Add fish oil as a Vitamin D source, and milk, for rickets prevention.
point: Rickets of the bones comes from not getting milk or sunlight: legs can become crooked and bones deformed; the best remedy is sunlight, plus milk and Vitamin D (found in fish oil). The book lists rickets twice, with different causes.
ref: Level B, Lesson 12: Food and Health, p.178

evidence: Not being able to see in dim light
point: Night blindness comes from too little Vitamin A: patients cannot see at night, their eyes get dry and eventually they go blind; children aged 2 to 5 are often affected.
ref: Level B, Lesson 12: Food and Health, p.177

evidence: Too much vitamin A or iron is a poison
point: Night blindness is prevented by breastfeeding for up to two years, and Vitamin A foods such as leafy vegetables, yellow and red fruits, milk, egg and liver; Vitamin A capsules are used only on a doctor's advice because too much is harmful.
ref: Level B, Lesson 12: Food and Health, p.177

evidence: too little vitamin C
add: Add cracked skin and mouth-corner sores from B-vitamin lack, alongside bleeding gums.
point: Dry cracked skin, wounds at the lips and corners of the mouth, and bleeding gums come from a lack of fruit, vegetables and vitamins; the cure is food rich in protein and vitamins.
ref: Level B, Lesson 12: Food and Health, p.178

evidence: Iodised salt is salt fortified with iodine.
point: Goitre, a swelling of the neck, is caused by too little iodine in food and is more common in hilly areas; it is prevented by using iodised salt, and old goitre can be removed by operation.
ref: Level B, Lesson 12: Food and Health, p.178

evidence: her baby's brain may not grow
point: If a pregnant woman lacks iodine, her child can be mentally challenged, dwarfed or deaf, so pregnant women should always eat food with iodised salt.
ref: Level B, Lesson 12: Food and Health, p.178

evidence: The polished rice had lost its vitamin B1.
point: Beri-Beri is caused by too little Vitamin B: it gives severe muscle pain, loss of appetite, poor digestion, cracked mouth corners and a rough red tongue.
ref: Level B, Lesson 12: Food and Health, p.178

evidence: thin, starchy porridge
add: Add top food for babies over six months: rice and lentil mix with milk, pulses, vegetables and fruit.
point: Growing children need proteins, so children over six months should be given top food with milk, such as rice and lentil mixture, pulses, oats, vegetables and fruits.
ref: Level B, Lesson 12: Food and Health, p.179

evidence: A girl with anaemia may be out of breath
add: Add that girls who have started periods need more iron-rich food such as ragi, bajra and greens.
point: Adolescent girls who have started menstruation should eat more iron-rich food to keep their blood level healthy.
ref: Level B, Lesson 12: Food and Health, p.179

evidence: why a baby, a pregnant woman, a worker and an old person need different diets
point: Pregnant and breastfeeding women should eat balanced food with calcium and iron, because the baby's health depends on what the mother eats.
ref: Level B, Lesson 12: Food and Health, p.180

evidence: does not always stop illness
add: Add that a sick person needs energy food plus protective vitamins and minerals to recover.
point: Sick people need food that gives strength and contains substances that help prevent other illnesses, because the body is weak during illness.
ref: Level B, Lesson 12: Food and Health, p.180

evidence: Kwashiorkor often begins after a child stops breastfeeding
add: Add: mother milk is the most easily available complete first food, complete when mother eats protein.
point: Mother's milk is the most easily available, healthy and complete food for a baby, and it is complete when the mother eats food containing protein.
ref: Level B, Lesson 12: Food and Health, p.180

evidence: Sprout whole pulses.
point: Nutritious food can be cheap: ragi and bajra have lots of iron and calcium, green beans and soya beans are the cheapest protein, sprouting beans adds more protein and vitamins, and jaggery has more iron than sugar.
ref: Level B, Lesson 12: Food and Health, p.180-181

evidence: Eaten together, each fills the other's gap.
add: Add: soaking maize in lime raises its vitamins and protein.
point: Unpolished cereals and whole pulses keep more vitamins, mixed cereals give different kinds of protein, and soaking corn in lime increases its vitamins and protein.
ref: Level B, Lesson 12: Food and Health, p.180-181

evidence: Cook to keep vitamins.
point: Cooking keeps vitamins and minerals when we cook vegetables and rice in less water, cut vegetables just before cooking, do not overcook them, and do not throw away the cooked rice water.
ref: Level B, Lesson 12: Food and Health, p.181

evidence: wash vegetables before cutting
add: Add: cook some food in iron pots, which adds iron, and eat seasonal produce.
point: Wash vegetables before cutting, eat seasonal fruits and vegetables, and cook vegetables in iron utensils, which adds iron to the food.
ref: Level B, Lesson 12: Food and Health, p.181

evidence: how microbes spoil it, and when to take extra care
point: Fungus and bacteria make food rot, and proper storage can keep food fresh for days or months, and it lets us enjoy seasonal produce later.
ref: Level B, Lesson 12: Food and Health, p.182

evidence: how drying, salt, sugar and cold keep it
point: Drying removes moisture so fungus cannot grow; sun drying is the cheapest way, and foods such as papad, peas, cereals, raisins and dried meat or fish are stored this way (meat and fish are salted first).
ref: Level B, Lesson 12: Food and Health, p.182-183

evidence: how drying, salt, sugar and cold keep it
add: Add village mud pots wrapped in wet cloth and sand, and farmers cold storage.
point: Refrigeration keeps food cool so fungus and bacteria do not grow; fridges, ice boxes and cold storage are used, and in villages food is kept cool in mud pots wrapped with cloth and sand.
ref: Level B, Lesson 12: Food and Health, p.183

evidence: a jar of mango pickle under oil
point: Salt, sugar, oil and spices stop fungus and bacteria: pickles have a top layer of oil that keeps them out, and amla, green mangoes, jams and jellies are kept with salt, sugar, vinegar or lemon juice.
ref: Level B, Lesson 12: Food and Health, p.183

evidence: with no chemical added
add: Add: preservative chemicals spoil food or harm the eater if too much or too little is used.
point: Chemicals can preserve food, but too much or too little can spoil it and harm the person who eats it, so they must be used with great caution.
ref: Level B, Lesson 12: Food and Health, p.183

evidence: Two pots of dal are boiled for the same time and covered.
point: High-temperature cooking kills bacteria, and poorly cooked food can cause food poisoning, with diarrhoea or vomiting.
ref: Level B, Lesson 12: Food and Health, p.183

evidence: Freezing kills microbes, so frozen food is safe for ever.
add: Add: food that has melted and been frozen again must not be frozen again.
point: Freezing stops fungus and bacteria from growing, but food that has melted should not be frozen again.
ref: Level B, Lesson 12: Food and Health, p.183

evidence: tell spoiled food from fermented food
add: Add canning: boil fruit, peas and tomatoes and seal them so air cannot reach them.
point: Canning boils fruits, peas and tomatoes and seals them so air cannot reach them, which keeps their nutrients; fermentation, the oldest method, is used for wine and vinegar.
ref: Level B, Lesson 12: Food and Health, p.184

evidence: thigh bone tied to the shin bone
add: Add: adults have 206 bones; the thigh bone is longest; the smallest bone is in the ear.
point: The adult human skeleton has 206 bones; the thigh bone is the longest and the smallest bone is behind the ear drum.
ref: Level B, Lesson 13: Internal Organs of the Human Body, p.191-192

evidence: I can explain the jobs of a skeleton
point: The skeleton gives shape and strength to the body, protects soft parts, and with muscles lets us walk and move our hands, feet and fingers.
ref: Level B, Lesson 13: Internal Organs of the Human Body, p.192

evidence: from the skull to the shin bone
add: Add: the skull is a box for the brain; 33 spine bones protect the spinal cord.
point: The skull is a box of strong bones that holds the brain; the spine is a column of 33 small and big bones through which the spinal cord carries messages from the brain to the body.
ref: Level B, Lesson 13: Internal Organs of the Human Body, p.192

evidence: The cage made by the ribs, the backbone
add: Add: twelve pairs of ribs, ten joined to the spine, guard the heart and lungs.
point: The rib cage of bones protects the lungs and heart, and the book says ten of the twelve ribs on each side are attached to the spine.
ref: Level B, Lesson 13: Internal Organs of the Human Body, p.192

evidence: Muscles in pairs, joints
add: Add movable joints (knee, elbow, wrist, fingers) versus immovable joints (skull).
point: A joint is where two bones meet: dynamic joints (knee, elbow, wrist, fingers) can move, while static joints (such as in the head) do not.
ref: Level B, Lesson 13: Internal Organs of the Human Body, p.192

evidence: Your heart is a muscle. It squeezes blood out
add: Add: the body has more than 600 muscles; heart and gut muscles work without thought.
point: Muscles join bones and let them move; the body has more than 600 muscles that can tighten and loosen, and the heart and intestines have muscles that work on their own.
ref: Level B, Lesson 13: Internal Organs of the Human Body, p.193

evidence: Your heart is a muscle. It squeezes blood out
add: Add voluntary muscles (hands, feet, fingers) versus involuntary ones (intestines, heart).
point: Voluntary muscles work when we wish (hands, feet, wrist, fingers), while involuntary muscles work on their own (intestines push food down, the heart pumps blood).
ref: Level B, Lesson 13: Internal Organs of the Human Body, p.193

evidence: The food tube from the mouth to the anus
point: The digestive system takes food in, digests it and removes waste; its main parts in order are mouth, food pipe, stomach, small intestine, big intestine, rectum and anus, with the liver as a gland that helps.
ref: Level B, Lesson 13: Internal Organs of the Human Body, p.194

evidence: A grown-up has 32 teeth.
point: In the mouth, teeth chew food and saliva from the saliva glands softens it; adults have 32 teeth.
ref: Level B, Lesson 13: Internal Organs of the Human Body, p.194

evidence: Gastric juice holds hydrochloric acid and an enzyme called pepsin.
add: Add: stomach acid kills many germs swallowed with food.
point: The stomach is a bag-like organ in the abdomen whose walls release juices that digest food and destroy harmful germs in it.
ref: Level B, Lesson 13: Internal Organs of the Human Body, p.194

evidence: Tiny finger-shaped bumps that cover the inner wall
point: The small intestine, about 7 metres long, finishes digestion, and its finger-like walls with many tiny blood vessels absorb the useful nutrients.
ref: Level B, Lesson 13: Internal Organs of the Human Body, p.194

evidence: what the large intestine and its bacteria do, and what faeces are made of
point: The big intestine absorbs water from the leftover food, and undigested waste (faeces) collects in the rectum and leaves through the anus.
ref: Level B, Lesson 13: Internal Organs of the Human Body, p.194

evidence: A yellow-green liquid made by the liver
add: Add: the liver is the body biggest gland, lying on the right side of the stomach.
point: The liver, the biggest gland in the body, lies on the right side of the stomach and makes bile, which goes to the small intestine to help digest food.
ref: Level B, Lesson 13: Internal Organs of the Human Body, p.194

evidence: In you, these are the nose, the windpipe, the lungs
add: Add the path: nose hairs clean air, larynx, trachea, two bronchi, then lungs.
point: Air enters through the nose, where tiny hairs clean it; it then passes the larynx (voice box), the trachea, and the two bronchi into the two lungs.
ref: Level B, Lesson 13: Internal Organs of the Human Body, p.195

evidence: One of the tiny air sacs at the ends of
point: Inside the lungs, the bronchi divide into tiny air bags called alveoli, which are wrapped in fine blood vessels that take oxygen from the air into the blood, which then goes to the heart.
ref: Level B, Lesson 13: Internal Organs of the Human Body, p.196

evidence: send carbon dioxide out
point: In the body, oxygen mixes with food elements to release energy, and carbon dioxide, a useless gas, is made and breathed out.
ref: Level B, Lesson 13: Internal Organs of the Human Body, p.196

evidence: Why you pant when you run
add: Add adult rate of 16 to 18 breaths a minute; exercise, illness and fever make it faster.
point: An adult breathes in 16 to 18 times a minute, and exercise, illness and fever make breathing faster.
ref: Level B, Lesson 13: Internal Organs of the Human Body, p.196

evidence: One of the tiny air sacs at the ends of
add: Add: smoking bidi or cigarettes damages the alveoli and causes breathing diseases.
point: Smoking bidi or cigarettes harms the alveoli and leads to respiratory (breathing) diseases.
ref: Level B, Lesson 13: Internal Organs of the Human Body, p.196

evidence: A grown-up's resting pulse is usually lower, about 60 to 90.
add: Add: heart is about the size of a fist; healthy rate 60 to 80, normal about 72 beats a minute.
point: The heart, about the size of a fist, works like a pump that expands and contracts all life; a healthy heart beats 60 to 80 times a minute, normally about 72.
ref: Level B, Lesson 13: Internal Organs of the Human Body, p.197

evidence: A chamber of the heart that receives blood
point: The heart has four chambers: the upper two are atria and the lower two are ventricles; the left and right sides never mix their blood.
ref: Level B, Lesson 13: Internal Organs of the Human Body, p.197

evidence: how blood and breath deliver oxygen to every cell
point: Blood circulates: impure blood (more carbon dioxide) reaches the right side and goes to the lungs, comes back with oxygen to the left side, and is pumped to the whole body, so the flow is continuous.
ref: Level B, Lesson 13: Internal Organs of the Human Body, p.197

evidence: Your kidneys clean your blood in the same way.
point: The two bean-shaped kidneys near the waist filter harmful waste and extra water from the blood, and keep the balance of water and mineral salts.
ref: Level B, Lesson 13: Internal Organs of the Human Body, p.198

evidence: Strong urine flows on to the bladder
add: Add the ureter (kidney to bladder) and the muscle ring that opens to pass urine.
point: Waste from the kidneys goes as urine down the ureter to the urinary bladder, which stores it until a ring of muscles opens to let it pass.
ref: Level B, Lesson 13: Internal Organs of the Human Body, p.198

point: The brain controls nearly every function of the body, and it is soft and safe inside the skull; its pink colour comes from many thin blood vessels that carry the oxygen it needs.
ref: Level B, Lesson 13: Internal Organs of the Human Body, p.199

point: The brain has three parts by function: one part controls muscles (walking, lifting), the lowest part controls automatic actions (heartbeat, breathing), and the largest part does speaking, hearing, smelling, thinking and remembering.
ref: Level B, Lesson 13: Internal Organs of the Human Body, p.199

evidence: is called semen
point: All living creatures have young to keep their species alive, and in humans two people, a male and a female, are needed to produce a child.
ref: Level B, Lesson 13: Internal Organs of the Human Body, p.200

evidence: It leaves through a tube in the penis.
point: Male reproductive organs include a pair of testicles outside the body, which make sperms; sperms mix with a fluid to form semen, which passes through the penis.
ref: Level B, Lesson 13: Internal Organs of the Human Body, p.200

evidence: Egg tube (fallopian tube)
point: Female reproductive organs lie in the lower abdomen: the uterus (protected by the pelvic bones), fallopian tubes about 4 inches long, ovaries with egg cells, and the vagina, and one mature egg comes out about every 28 days.
ref: Level B, Lesson 13: Internal Organs of the Human Body, p.200-201

evidence: Egg tube (fallopian tube)
point: When a sperm fertilises the mature egg in the fallopian tube, the fertilised egg sticks to the uterus wall and the baby develops; if no fertilisation happens, the uterus lining leaves the body as menstruation every month.
ref: Level B, Lesson 13: Internal Organs of the Human Body, p.201

evidence: Colds, chickenpox, cholera, malaria and tuberculosis are infectious.
point: Diseases are divided into infectious diseases, which spread from one person to another through air, infected food and water, mosquitoes and flies, and non-infectious diseases, which do not spread between people.
ref: Level B, Lesson 14: Common Diseases - their reasons, prevention and protection from them, p.207

evidence: How a virus takes over a cell
point: Many infectious diseases are caused by bacteria and viruses, which cannot be seen with the naked eye and need a microscope to be seen.
ref: Level B, Lesson 14: Common Diseases - their reasons, prevention and protection from them, p.208

evidence: Colds, chickenpox, cholera, malaria and tuberculosis are infectious.
point: The book groups diseases: infectious ones include tuberculosis, tetanus, polio, cholera, typhoid, HIV/AIDS, cold, flu, measles, small pox, malaria, dengue and mumps; non-infectious ones include gout, heart attack, epilepsy, cancer, cataract, glaucoma, asthma, allergy, diabetes and goitre.
ref: Level B, Lesson 14: Common Diseases - their reasons, prevention and protection from them, p.208

evidence: reach water, hands, flies or food
point: Cholera spreads through flies, dirty water and infected food, and causes loose watery stools, vomiting and mild fever that can lead to dangerous loss of water; protection includes covered food, clean water, soap, and burying the patient's stool.
ref: Level B, Lesson 14: Common Diseases - their reasons, prevention and protection from them, p.209

evidence: lays eggs in clean standing water
point: Malaria, dengue and elephantiasis spread when mosquitoes carry disease bacteria from one person to another; symptoms include fever, chills and headache, and protection means avoiding mosquitoes and not letting water collect around the home.
ref: Level B, Lesson 14: Common Diseases - their reasons, prevention and protection from them, p.210

evidence: Food they cook can still make others ill.
add: Add typhoid symptoms (fever rising slowly, vomiting, diarrhoea), boiled water, and isolating the patient.
point: Typhoid is an intestinal disease caused by contaminated food and water, with high fever that rises slowly, vomiting, diarrhoea and headache; protection includes clean food and water, boiled water and isolating the patient.
ref: Level B, Lesson 14: Common Diseases - their reasons, prevention and protection from them, p.210

evidence: Colds, chickenpox, cholera, malaria and tuberculosis are infectious.
add: Add TB signs (mild fever, cough, chest pain), doctor for a cough over two weeks, long treatment.
point: Tuberculosis (TB) usually affects the lungs and spreads easily to weak or malnourished children and people near a patient; symptoms are mild continuous fever, cough and chest pain, and it needs regular long treatment.
ref: Level B, Lesson 14: Common Diseases - their reasons, prevention and protection from them, p.211

evidence: cholera, typhoid, diarrhoea, dysentery
add: Add dysentery (blood or phlegm in stool), dehydration danger, and breastfeeding for babies.
point: Diarrhoea is loose watery stool and dysentery has blood or phlegm in it; repeated stool loss causes dehydration, which can be fatal, and babies are safest when breastfed instead of bottle-fed.
ref: Level B, Lesson 14: Common Diseases - their reasons, prevention and protection from them, p.211-212

evidence: a child sneezing
add: Add: getting wet does not cause colds; vitamin C foods help; sleep and good food protect.
point: Cold and flu spread through the air when a patient sneezes; they cause sneezing, coughing, runny nose and mild fever, and good sleep, nourishing food and vitamin C fruits help prevent them, while getting wet does not cause them.
ref: Level B, Lesson 14: Common Diseases - their reasons, prevention and protection from them, p.212

evidence: some kinds of pneumonia
add: Add pneumonia signs (fast breathing, chest pain, coloured phlegm, high fever) and that it can follow chickenpox, flu or asthma.
point: Pneumonia is a dangerous lung disease that can follow chickenpox, whooping cough, flu or asthma; it causes fast breathing, chest pain, coughing with coloured phlegm and high fever, and is very dangerous for children.
ref: Level B, Lesson 14: Common Diseases - their reasons, prevention and protection from them, p.212-213

evidence: passes from person to person in blood, in sex between grown-ups
add: Add prevention: condoms, single-use needles, tested blood, and free tests in hospitals.
point: AIDS is a loss of the body's strength to fight disease, caused by the HIV virus (Human Immuno Deficiency Virus); it spreads through sex, infected blood and shared needles, and from mother to child, and it can be stopped by awareness, condoms, blood tests and single-use needles, with free tests in hospitals.
ref: Level B, Lesson 14: Common Diseases - their reasons, prevention and protection from them, p.213-214

evidence: heart and blood vessels in red
add: Add heart attack: fat blocks the vessels; pain to left arm, sweating; less ghee and oil helps.
point: Heart stroke, more likely in older people who eat greasy food, smoke or have high blood pressure, happens when fat blocks the blood vessels so blood cannot reach the heart; chest pain spreading to the left arm and sweating are signs, and simple food with less ghee and oil helps prevent it.
ref: Level B, Lesson 14: Common Diseases - their reasons, prevention and protection from them, p.215

evidence: Malaria, anaemia, diabetes and asthma are all diseases
add: Add diabetes signs (slow-healing wounds, blurred sight, frequent urination) and prevention by healthy weight and yearly checks after 40.
point: Diabetes is a lifestyle disease that can also run in families and shows up as blood sugar rising; signs include wounds that heal slowly, blurred sight, frequent urination, and dry hands and feet, and prevention means avoiding obesity and checking blood after age 40.
ref: Level B, Lesson 14: Common Diseases - their reasons, prevention and protection from them, p.215-216

add: Add smoking and chewing tobacco as cancer risks, and early signs: lumps, reddish skin, later pain or bleeding.
point: Cancer can appear on any part of the body; smoking can cause lung and lip cancer, chewing tobacco raises the risk of mouth cancer, and early signs are lumps, reddish skin and later pain or bleeding.
ref: Level B, Lesson 14: Common Diseases - their reasons, prevention and protection from them, p.216

evidence: A safe preparation that shows the body a
point: A little precaution is better than many treatments: nutritious food, vaccination and clean homes and surroundings protect people from many diseases.
ref: Level B, Lesson 14: Common Diseases - their reasons, prevention and protection from them, p.217

evidence: washed with soap and running water for 15 minutes
add: Add daily handwashing with soap after toilet and before meals, daily bath, brushing teeth, no spitting.
point: Personal cleanliness means washing hands with soap after the toilet and before meals, bathing daily, brushing teeth after meals and in the morning, not spitting on the ground, and keeping children away from domestic animals.
ref: Level B, Lesson 14: Common Diseases - their reasons, prevention and protection from them, p.217

evidence: a child sneezing
add: Add: cover the mouth with a cloth when coughing or sneezing, since TB, measles and flu travel through air.
point: Diseases such as TB, chickenpox, measles, flu, cold, cough, pneumonia and diphtheria spread through the air when someone coughs or sneezes, so cover the mouth with a cloth or handkerchief.
ref: Level B, Lesson 14: Common Diseases - their reasons, prevention and protection from them, p.217

evidence: Two pots of dal are boiled for the same time and covered.
point: Food and drink must be kept clean: drink boiled and then cooled water (especially for small children and during outbreaks), keep food covered, wash fruits and vegetables before eating, and avoid stale or open food.
ref: Level B, Lesson 14: Common Diseases - their reasons, prevention and protection from them, p.217

evidence: Fresh water and salt water: why so little of Earth's water can be drunk
add: Add: keep tanks, wells and rivers clean, toilets at home, proper garbage disposal, and no standing water for mosquitoes.
point: Clean surroundings protect water sources and stop breeding: keep tanks, wells and rivers clean, keep toilets at home, dispose of garbage properly and do not let water collect, since mosquitoes breed in it.
ref: Level B, Lesson 14: Common Diseases - their reasons, prevention and protection from them, p.218

evidence: how they spread and how to prevent them
add: Add: skin infections spread by touch, clothes and bedding; healthy children sleep apart; carers wash after nursing.
point: Diseases such as itching, eczema, TB and venereal diseases spread by touching a patient, wearing his clothes or sleeping on his bed, so healthy children should sleep apart and the carer should clean up after nursing.
ref: Level B, Lesson 14: Common Diseases - their reasons, prevention and protection from them, p.218

evidence: measles, polio, tetanus, typhoid and some kinds of pneumonia
point: Vaccines protect children from TB, tetanus, diphtheria, whooping cough, polio, chickenpox and typhoid, so children should be vaccinated.
ref: Level B, Lesson 14: Common Diseases - their reasons, prevention and protection from them, p.218

evidence: Tobacco smoke, dirty air, alcohol
add: Add alcohol causing liver cirrhosis and harming the whole family.
point: Drinking alcohol causes liver diseases such as cirrhosis and harms the whole family, not just the drinker.
ref: Level B, Lesson 14: Common Diseases - their reasons, prevention and protection from them, p.218

evidence: Tobacco smoke, dirty air, alcohol
add: Add smoking harms: lung and lip cancer, breathing diseases, pneumonia in children, harm to unborn babies.
point: Smoking bidi or cigarettes raises the risk of lung and lip cancer, causes breathing diseases and ulcers, can be fatal for asthma patients, makes children of smokers more prone to pneumonia, and harms an unborn child; money spent on these habits could buy nutritious food.
ref: Level B, Lesson 14: Common Diseases - their reasons, prevention and protection from them, p.219

evidence: Waste after the bin: what rots, what stays, and where it all goes
point: Degradable (organic) waste is garbage that rots and mixes with soil, such as dust, paper, leaves, old clothes, vegetable peels and leftover food.
ref: Level B, Lesson 15: Garbage and Waste and its Disposal, p.226

evidence: Waste after the bin: what rots, what stays, and where it all goes
point: Non-degradable (inorganic) waste, such as iron nails, glass, plastic and polythene, does not rot for a long time and stays on the ground as it was.
ref: Level B, Lesson 15: Garbage and Waste and its Disposal, p.226

evidence: Waste after the bin: what rots, what stays, and where it all goes
point: Proper disposal means separating degradable from non-degradable waste so that each can be re-used, rather than dumping it in a pit, well, pond or river.
ref: Level B, Lesson 15: Garbage and Waste and its Disposal, p.226-227

evidence: Waste after the bin: what rots, what stays, and where it all goes
point: Rotting waste can be made into compost manure in a pit in a corner of the courtyard or garden, kept moist with water, and used for flower-pots and gardens.
ref: Level B, Lesson 15: Garbage and Waste and its Disposal, p.227

evidence: An aluminium can sold as scrap can
point: Non-degradable waste is collected by scrap collectors, who pay for it, and it is melted or burnt in factories to make useful items, which is a form of re-use.
ref: Level B, Lesson 15: Garbage and Waste and its Disposal, p.227

evidence: what rots, what stays
add: Add two labelled bins at home, one for organic and one for inorganic waste; hospital colour codes optional.
point: Waste should be kept in separate dustbins: one for organic and one for inorganic waste; hospitals use green for organic, red for glass vials, bottles and plastic, and black for rotten things.
ref: Level B, Lesson 15: Garbage and Waste and its Disposal, p.228

evidence: loose in the environment
add: Define environment: everything around us, made by nature or by people; proper disposal keeps it clean.
point: The environment is everything around us, whether made by nature or by people, and proper disposal of garbage keeps it clean and free from pollution.
ref: Level B, Lesson 15: Garbage and Waste and its Disposal, p.228

point: Burning tyres, plastic and polythene pollutes the air, and garbage left on fields makes soil barren; these pollutants enter our bodies when we breathe and make us sick.
ref: Level B, Lesson 15: Garbage and Waste and its Disposal, p.229

evidence: when a river, a pond or a well 'looks clear'
point: Factory and household waste dumped into rivers and drains, and garbage carried by rain into water sources, pollutes drinking water and irrigation water, which then carries disease to people and crops.
ref: Level B, Lesson 15: Garbage and Waste and its Disposal, p.229

evidence: what rots, what stays
add: Add habits: no littering or spitting, no burning tyres or polythene, compost at home, and teach children.
point: Cleanliness begins with our own habits: do not litter or spit, do not use polythene or burn tyres, make compost from organic waste, and teach children to keep clean, because a clean environment keeps us healthy.
ref: Level B, Lesson 15: Garbage and Waste and its Disposal, p.229-230
